#5456. University of Phoenix White Paper Examines Workplace AI Training Gaps and Challenges of Responsible Workplace Adoption

Authors Dr. Louise Underdahl and Dr. Alma Gojkovic draw on Career Optimism IndexÂ® findings and accounting-sector research to explore role-specific training needs and organizational approaches to AI integration.

PHOENIX, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies has published a new white paper, "Learning to Use AI: Challenges and Opportunities," by Louise Underdahl, Ph.D., and Alma Gojkovic, DBA, examining how organizations can better support employees learning to use artificial intelligence (AI) as workplace adoption expands. Drawing on the 2026 Career Optimism IndexÂ®, Gojkovic's 2025 qualitative doctoral research on AI implementation in accounting and additional scholarly literature, the authors examine shortcomings in workplace AI training, risks associated with unstructured adoption and approaches to improving organizational implementation.

What does research reveal about workplace AI learning?

The white paper draws on findings from the 2026 Career Optimism IndexÂ®, a national study of U.S. workers and employers, identifying a gap between employees' AI learning activities and organizational guidance:

The authors examine these findings alongside research on AI integration, including Gojkovic's 2025 qualitative exploratory case study of accounting managers, accounting staff and AI technology project leaders in selected organizations in the southwestern United States.

Participants in that study described AI training as frequently too general, too brief or insufficiently connected to specific accounting responsibilities. They also identified limited opportunities for ongoing feedback, practical application and post-training support.

"The accounting professionals in my research described a need for training that went beyond introducing AI tools," said Gojkovic. "They wanted practical examples relevant to their responsibilities, opportunities to apply what they learned and ongoing support as new technologies became part of their daily work. Their experiences highlight why role-specific training deserves greater attention."

Why does unstructured AI adoption create organizational challenges?

The authors also examine a broader organizational challenge: Traditional approaches to technology implementation may not adequately account for AI systems that adapt and evolve through use. Drawing on research involving complex adaptive systems, the paper explores how staged learning, continuous feedback and coordinated changes across people, processes and technology can inform more effective AI integration.

"Learning to use AI is not solely a question of acquiring technical skills," said Underdahl. "Organizations also need to consider how employees learn, how new technologies change established practices and what support structures are needed for responsible use. Effective integration requires attention to people, processes and organizational culture alongside the technology itself."

Strategies for strengthening workplace AI training and adoption

The authors discuss several research-informed approaches organizations can consider when developing AI learning and implementation practices:

Taken together, the research points to the importance of treating AI adoption as an ongoing organizational learning process rather than a one-time technology implementation, with employees, managers and organizational leaders contributing to responsible integration, supported by targeted training, effective governance, and strategic planning.

The full white paper is available on the Research Hub.

"Learning to Use AI: Challenges and Opportunities," by Louise Underdahl, Ph.D., and Alma Gojkovic, DBA, synthesizes findings from workforce survey research, a previously conducted qualitative study of AI implementation in accounting and additional scholarly literature. The publication examines workplace AI training challenges, unanticipated consequences of adoption and research-informed strategies for organizational implementation.

The Career Optimism IndexÂ® findings cited in the paper are drawn from online surveys of 5,000 U.S. adults age 18 and older who were working or wished to be working, and 1,000 U.S. employers involved in hiring and workplace decisions, conducted Jan. 21 â Feb. 6, 2026.

The white paper is an analysis of existing research and does not report a new national survey or independently evaluate the effectiveness of an AI training intervention.

Underdahl is a doctoral instructor at University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies and a research fellow with the College's Center for Educational and Instructional Technology Research (CEITR). Her scholarship addresses workforce attitudes, professional development, mentoring and educational research. She earned her PhD, Master of Public Administration and Master of Science in Library Science from the University of Southern California and her bachelor's degree from the University of California, Los Angeles.

Gojkovic is a University of Phoenix doctoral graduate whose research examines artificial intelligence adoption in accounting industry practices. Her doctoral research explores how organizational leadership, employee training, governance policies, and employee experiences influence the implementation of emerging AI technologies into accounting workflows. Her scholarly interests include AI-driven innovation, organizational change management, technology adoption, and the evolving role of accounting professionals in a digital business environment. She has professional experience in information technology and in the accounting industry, with the interest in advancing AI and emerging technologies into accounting practices and business transformation. She earned her Doctor of Business Administration (DBA) and Master of Science in Accountancy from University of Phoenix, and her bachelor's degree from Arizona State University.

#5455. D-Matrix bets stacked DRAM can solve inference’s memory bandwidth problem

As artificial intelligence workloads shift to inference, memory bandwidth decides whether hardware generates tokens quickly or sits idle. D-Matrix Corp. is answering with Raptor, a second-generation chip stacking 3D DRAM beneath its compute logic.

AI infrastructure has become a systems game, and winners combine memory, interconnect and software into cohesive designs, according to Satyam Srivastava (pictured), fellow at d-Matrix.

“It’s no longer a chip problem. Chip plays a part of it. Memory bandwidth is a fundamental advantage that has to be solved,” Srivastava said. “The next is energy efficiency. The next is interconnect efficiency. The next is software cohesiveness.”

Srivastava spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed d-Matrix’s Raptor chip and its stacked 3D DRAM, inference memory bandwidth and the shift toward heterogeneous computing. (* Disclosure below.)

D-Matrix proves each risky technology on a test chip first. Jayhawk proved die-to-die connectivity, and Jayhawk II validated digital in-memory computing. The Corsair accelerator combined both and entered full production earlier this year, Srivastava explained.

“Fast forward, we have the Pavehawk chip, test chip, which is proving out 3D DRAM stacked underneath the logic die, which serves as the core technology for Raptor, which is our second-generation chip coming out next year,” Srivastava said.

Stacking keeps the distributed memory architecture intact but moves memory cells onto a separate layer rather than consuming logic die area. Data travels a short distance and never crosses an interposer. That puts 3D DRAM in a new tier between SRAM and high-bandwidth memory, Srivastava said.

“So you’re getting 10 times higher energy efficiency compared to HBM, 10 times higher bandwidth compared to HBM, where it sits in between SRAM and HBM in terms of capacity,” Srivastava said.

Pairing a Corsair-based server with an existing Hopper GPU fleet can raise utilization from about 20% to as much as 80%, meaning more tokens per dollar, Srivastava noted. D-Matrix has also adopted NVLink Fusion rackscale infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. to connect its accelerators to Nvidia’s AI factories.

“For us, it unlocks the opportunity to participate in a very established ecosystem, the world’s most popular AI factory. We get access to a very hardened design of an MGX rack,” Srivastava said.

The partnership points toward heterogeneous computing, where software orchestrates GPUs, CPUs and accelerators such as Raptor as one system, with the cluster as the unit of computing, Srivastava explained.

“So think of a chip, but that chip is an entire cluster and it has many different hardware units,” Srivastava said. “Some are GPUs, some are CPUs, some are ASIC accelerators, and you can use whichever one you like to serve the needs of the workload the best.”

#5454. Mortgage delinquencies rise to 4.42% in Q3 2026

Mortgage delinquencies increased in Q3 2026 to 4.42%, MBA reported, with serious delinquencies rising to 2.12% without accounting for seasonality. FHA and VA foreclosure rates reached 1.89% and 1.06%, respectively, their highest levels since 2017 and 2016.   AI Summary

Mortgage delinquencies increased in the third quarter of 2026, with the share of loans at least one payment past due rising to 4.42%. That’s according to the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA)’s National Delinquency Survey, released Thursday.

The seasonally adjusted delinquency rate for one- to four-unit residential properties was up 5 basis points from the second quarter and 43 bps from a year earlier.

Foreclosure starts also increased, with the share of loans entering the foreclosure process rising 1 basis point from the previous quarter to 0.21%. The percentage of loans already in foreclosure reached 0.71%, up 4 bps quarterly and 21 bps year over year.

“Loans 90 days or more late or in foreclosure increased for the fifth consecutive quarter and are 51 basis points higher than the third quarter of 2025,” said Marina Walsh, MBA’s vice president and head of industry analysis.

Walsh said the deterioration in government-backed loans is contributing to higher foreclosure activity. The Federal Housing Administration (FHA) foreclosure rate reached 1.89%, its highest level since the first quarter of 2017, while the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) foreclosure rate climbed to 1.06%, its highest since Q4 2016.

By delinquency stage, the 30-day rate increased 4 basis points from the previous quarter to 2.25%, while the 60-day rate rose 1 bps to 0.74%. The 90-day delinquency rate remained unchanged at 1.43%.

Performance varied by loan type. The conventional mortgage delinquency rate increased by 1 basis point from the second quarter to 2.73%, while the FHA rate declined 5 bps to 11.74%. The VA delinquency rate rose 11 bps to 5%.

All three loan categories posted annual increases. Conventional delinquencies were up 11 bps from a year earlier, while FHA delinquencies increased 96 bps and VA delinquencies rose 50 bps.

The seriously delinquent rate, which includes loans at least 90 days past due or in the foreclosure process, reached 2.12% on a nonseasonally adjusted basis. That was up 6 basis points from the second quarter and 51 bps year over year.

FHA loans recorded the largest annual deterioration in serious delinquencies, with the rate rising 197 basis points. The rate increased 13 basis points for conventional loans and 60 basis points for VA loans.

The five states with the largest quarterly increases in overall mortgage delinquencies were Wyoming, up 72 basis points, followed by West Virginia and Louisiana, both up 32 basis points. Arkansas saw its rate increase by 31 basis points, while Kentucky’s rose by 27 bps.

Walsh said the overall mortgage delinquency rate closely tracks the national unemployment rate, which stood at 4.1% in October.

Although the labor market has remained resilient, Walsh pointed to several pressures on household finances, including wage growth lagging inflation, declining personal savings, and rising balances on credit cards, auto loans and student loans.

Borrowers who took out mortgages in recent years at higher interest rates may also face affordability challenges that make timely payments more difficult, Walsh said. Changes to mortgage relief programs over the past year, including the removal of some COVID-era flexibilities, could be adding to financial pressures for some homeowners.

#5453. /C O R R E C T I O N - Ignite Reading/

In the news release, District leaders from across the country commit to the First Grade Promise, set March 2027 for first national First Grade Promise Week, issued 18-Nov-2026 by Ignite Reading over PR Newswire, we are advised by the company that changes have been made. The complete, corrected release follows, with additional details at the end:

Educators who gathered on Nov. 5 say waiting until 3rd grade to fix reading costs children two years they can't get back.

OAKLAND, Calif., Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- For decades, schools have treated 3rd grade as the year that decides whether a student becomes a reader. District leaders from across the country came together last week and declared 3rd grade is two years too late.

On Nov. 5, 56 district leaders and literacy leaders from six states met in Boston for Convene 2026. The national gathering, hosted by Ignite Reading, centered on the First Grade Promise, a commitment launched in 2025 to get every child reading on grade level by the end of 1st grade.

Leaders spent the day-long event pinpointing where 1st graders slip through the cracks in a system and drafting their commitments to close reading gaps early, when intervention has the most lasting impact. Ignite Reading also announced the first national First Grade Promise Week, set for March 1â5, 2027.

The window to get a child on track closes long before the 3rd grade tests most states still use to measure reading success. A 2026 NWEA analysis tracked more than 400,000 children from the start of kindergarten. Kindergartners who started school reading below benchmark have a 1 in 4 chance of reading proficiently by the end of 3rd grade. For children still in the bottom 20% in the spring of 1st grade, those odds fell to 1 in 40.

Kareem Weaver, Co-Founder & Executive Director of FULCRUM, stated, "If we wait until 3rd grade to intervene, we are asking 8-to-9-year-olds to carry the burden of a 'wait-to-fail' model. Fixing reading gaps isn't about catching kids up; it's about giving every child the foundational tools needed to read on time, 1st grade. That shift in timing changes the trajectory of a child's life, and it's key to securing their basic civil rights."

District leaders from Georgia, California, and Massachusetts spoke throughout the day, sharing how they're keeping the promise in their own communities.

In Georgia, where state reading tests begin in 3rd grade, Savannah-Chatham County Public School System moved its reading intervention funding to 1st grade this year. The district has also set a public goal of 95 percent of 3rd graders reading on grade level within five years, up from 53 percent. District leaders joined Weaver to detail how they built the case for the shift.

"Foundational literacy unlocks a child's ability to achieve unlimited possibilities. We owe it to our students, families, and community to ensure that all students are reading on grade level, and that promise begins in kindergarten and 1st grade," said Shraddha Nunziata, Senior Director of Initiatives & Special Projects of Savannah-Chatham County Public School System. "Ignite Reading is a crucial partner in ensuring our youngest readers have the support they need to become strong readers, but we have also strengthened and streamlined structured literacy instruction in the classroom, so the progress our students are making is thanks to our dedicated and talented teachers. By concentrating efforts in the earliest grades, our intervention burden decreases in second grade and beyond, and students are set up to succeed in all subject areas."

Leaders from California's San Bruno Park School District and Massachusetts' Chelsea Public Schools took the stage to detail their district efforts to ensure families are active participants in a system that gets 1st graders reading. Attendees heard how Chelsea's family liaisons are trained in literacy initiatives so they can answer parents' questions about screening and report cards, and how San Bruno Park leverages students' own excitement about their early literacy intervention to gain buy-in from parents and guardians.

"Parent engagement has been recognized for years as a critical factor in student achievement. To build engagement, we must cultivate relationships with families that are built on trust by supporting them in learning to navigate the school system and helping them remove any barriers that may impede their ability to support their child," said Michelle Graham, Director of Teaching, Learning and Intervention at San Bruno Park School District.

"Learning to read is not easy for many children. These students need explicit, systematic instruction and additional support to become confident, successful readers. It is essential that we share clear, meaningful information with families so they understand how their child is progressing, where they may need additional support, and how we can work together to ensure every child has the opportunity to acquire the skills they need to become proficient readers," said Katelyn Webber-Schubmehl, PK-8 Literacy and Humanities Director at Chelsea Public Schools.

First Grade Promise Week will take the question district leaders worked on in Boston to communities across the country: what will it take for every child to read by the end of 1st grade? National speakers and the full program will be announced in January.

Anyone can take the First Grade Promise pledge now at www.firstgradepromise.org.

The First Grade Promise is a national commitment to make sure every child reads on grade level by the end of 1st grade, when reading gaps are still small enough to close. It is open to anyone, from district leaders to parents. First Grade Promise Week takes place March 1â5, 2027. Learn more and take the pledge at www.firstgradepromise.org.

Ignite Reading is an early literacy intervention that closes students' reading gaps when it matters most, before they turn into a lifetime of catching up. Students in school districts nationwide receive daily, one-to-one intervention that's aligned to the Science of Reading and personalized to master the exact skills they're missing. The results stick: Johns Hopkins University researchers found 17 in 20 students who reached benchmark with Ignite Reading were still on benchmark a year later.

#5452. Trump's accounts bought shares of Palantir and SpaceX near federal contract awards

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The September disclosure lists Nvidia trades as well; the White House says independent managers make all investment decisions

President Donald Trump outside the White House. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump's investment accounts reported purchases of shares of Palantir $PLTR and SpaceX in September, in the weeks around federal contract awards to both companies, according to a disclosure released Thursday.

The filing lists Palantir purchases of $15,001 to $50,000 on Sept. 2 and $1,001 to $15,000 on Sept. 9. The Department of Housing and Urban Development awarded Palantir a $10.4 million delivery order that started Sept. 16, according to USAspending.gov. The order covers an AI-powered grant intelligence platform. On Sept. 29, the Department of Homeland Security awarded Palantir a $32.1 million software license contract.

Palantir CEO Alex Karp took part on Sept. 29 in a White House session on artificial intelligence, alongside Trump, Elon Musk, Nvidia $NVDA CEO Jensen Huang and several other tech industry leaders, according to CNBC.

For SpaceX, the filing shows purchases of $1,001 to $15,000 on Sept. 9 and $15,001 to $50,000 on Sept. 24. The accounts also bought $100,001 to $250,000 in SpaceX debt on Sept. 1, according to CNBC. NASA said on Sept. 18 that it was extending its SpaceX deal by $946 million, which pays for three more crewed flights to the International Space Station and lifts the contract’s overall worth to $5.92 billion, according to CNBC.

The filing shows four Nvidia purchases totaling $152,004 to $380,000, including two on Sept. 2 worth as much as $350,000 combined, according to CNBC. The others were purchases of $1,001 to $15,000 on Sept. 9 and Sept. 10. The accounts also sold $1,001 to $15,000 in Nvidia shares on Sept. 24, the day Huang attended Trump’s state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping, CNBC said.

Reuters put the September Nvidia purchases at as much as $265,000. The filing reports values in ranges, so exact amounts are unclear, according to both outlets. CNBC said the trades push the number of Trump’s Nvidia transactions since early 2025 to a minimum of 108.

Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Nov. 12 after reports of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. authorities suspect of intelligence ties to Beijing.

CNBC's analysis of the 25-page filing tallied 751 trades, both buys and sells, with a combined value of about $40.9 million to $148.1 million.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle said independent managers run Trump's portfolio, and that the president and his family have no say over trades. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers," Ingle told CNBC. CNBC said it found nothing showing that Trump directed the transactions, or that his managers had advance knowledge of government decisions.

#5451. Why Compass wants the MLS antitrust dispute out of New York

Seven MLSs are urging an SDNY judge to retain their declaratory judgment case against Compass over MLS cooperation and listing submission rules. Compass argues the filing was anticipatory and seeks dismissal or severance and transfer to multiple home districts.  AI Summary

Compass International Holdings and a group of seven MLS plaintiffs are asking a federal judge in New York to decide if and where their antitrust battle over MLS cooperation and listing submission rules should proceed. The parties filed dueling letters earlier this month laying out competing narratives on forum shopping, efficiency and control over nationwide litigation.

In a Nov. 13 letter, Compass said it will seek to dismiss a consolidated declaratory judgment action filed by seven multiple listing services headquartered in Arizona, California, Colorado and North Carolina, or, alternatively, to sever and transfer each MLS’s claims to the district where Compass has brought its own antitrust case against that MLS.

The lawsuit was filed in the Southern District of New York (SDNY) by Arizona Regional MLS (ARMLS), OneKey MLS, MLSListings, Bridge MLS, Canopy MLS, Recolorado, Hive MLS and Doorify MLS after Compass sent letters to MLSs across the country in September demanding that they stop fining agents for publicly marketing office exclusive listings.

The MLSs are seeking declarations that their rules comply with Section 1 of the Sherman Act and state antitrust statutes, and an injunction preventing Compass from “bringing or pursuing any claim” against them over those rules, according to the amended complaint.

Compass told the court the MLSs’ consolidated suit is an “improper anticipatory filing” under the Declaratory Judgment Act. Citing prior legal precedent, Compass argued that courts may decline jurisdiction when declaratory relief is used “for procedural fencing.” The company pointed to its September demand letters, the sue‑by deadlines it set, and a series of deadline extensions it granted as part of what it characterizes as a good‑faith attempt to resolve the dispute short of litigation.

In the letter, Compass said counsel for ARMLS, Doorify MLS and Hive MLS requested a draft release and then sought additional time, citing illness and scheduling constraints, before filing this lawsuit in New York without substantively responding to the demands. Other MLSs, including MLSListings, BridgeMLS, REcolorado and Canopy MLS, also requested extensions to respond to the demand letter, Compass said.

Compass alleges the MLSs used those extensions to prepare the SDNY filing and then sued the day after certain extended deadlines expired. Compass also emphasized that it has since filed “home‑district” actions against each MLS in its own federal district, along with additional suits against other MLSs.

Since those damages claims cannot be resolved by declaratory relief alone and involve additional parties and provisions, Compass argued in its letter that the SDNY case would not “settle the controversy.”

However, as an alternative to dismissal, Compass is asking the court to sever each MLS’s claims and transfer them to the districts where the company’s separate antitrust suits are pending: Arizona, Northern California, Colorado and the Western and Eastern Districts of North Carolina.

Compass said the MLSs themselves allege they act “independently,” operate in distinct regional markets, have different governing boards and maintain non‑identical rules. Having a shared adversary in Compass and a similar form demand letter do not make their policies a single transaction or occurrence, the company told the court.

In a response letter sent on Wednesday, counsel for the MLS plaintiffs urged the court to keep the case and deny Compass’s anticipated motions. The MLSs argue that the SDNY suit is a textbook use of the Declaratory Judgment Act and that Compass, from its New York headquarters, orchestrated a “nationwide campaign” against cooperation rules that should be resolved in a single forum.

The MLSs characterize Compass’s pre‑suit communications differently, saying the company presented only two options: abandon their cooperation rules entirely in exchange for what they describe as a “toothless” release that left them under a “perpetual threat” of future litigation, or face antitrust lawsuits without clarity as to timing or venue.

The MLSs also dispute Compass’s forum‑shopping argument, emphasizing that they sued the brokerage in its home district and in the same court where Compass chose to litigate a separate cooperation‑rule case against Zillow.

By contrast, they say Compass’s 15-case strategy across 11 districts invites inconsistent outcomes and “massive inefficiencies.”

The MLS plaintiffs also pushed back on Compass’s bid to sever and transfer their claims. They argue their joinder meets federal procedure rules because each MLS plaintiff faces the same type of challenge from a single defendant over listing-submission rules that, while not identical, share common structure and legal issues.

Regarding the possibility of transferring the case, the MLSs say Compass cannot meet its burden to show, by clear and convincing evidence, that moving the case would serve the convenience of parties and witnesses and the interests of justice. They feel that their choice of Compass’s home forum is entitled to substantial deference, particularly because Compass’s executives and documents are in New York.

It remains to be seen how the court will rule on this issue. However, the ruling will help determine where and how quickly federal courts address the legality of MLS rules that require brokers to share publicly marketed listings with other brokers through the cooperative database of the MLS.

#5450. Hackers Hijack 178 Major Websites, Including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, and Ledger

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hackers have turned some of the world’s most recognizable websites into potential crypto theft traps after compromising a third-party platform used by 178 major organizations. The attack injected malicious JavaScript through Optimizely, a website experimentation platform trusted by companies including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, IKEA, and crypto hardware wallet maker Ledger.

Visitors could unknowingly load malware simply by opening an affected webpage, and the consequences go far beyond stolen browsing data. The malicious code can replace crypto wallet addresses copied to the clipboard, redirecting payments straight into attackers’ wallets. Security researchers have already identified $7,040 in crypto received by wallets linked to the campaign.

🚨 BREAKING: Ledger and 177 other major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, and Salesforce, were affected by a massive JavaScript attack.The malware stole cryptocurrency, payment card details, and user data, while also targeting iPhones with exploit kits.

The investigation by cybersecurity firm Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets belonging to 178 organizations after examining 1,611 Optimizely scripts. The malware operated through trusted website infrastructure, making the attack particularly dangerous. Rather than breaking into every company’s servers individually, attackers injected malicious code into Optimizely customer projects.

Affected websites continued loading JavaScript through Optimizely’s legitimate content delivery network. Visitors had little reason to suspect that a familiar website was serving malicious instructions. This is a dangerous clipboard hijacking mechanism.

The malware searched webpages for crypto wallet addresses and replaced legitimate destinations with addresses controlled by attackers. It could also intercept copied addresses, meaning someone browsing an affected website could potentially paste a fraudulent wallet address elsewhere.

The attack targeted several major crypto networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, and Litecoin.

A victim could believe they were sending funds to an exchange, another wallet, or a friend. Instead, the transaction could land directly in an attacker’s wallet.

Report URI identified $7,040 in receipts across attacker-controlled wallets by November 16. The funds included Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, TRON, and stablecoins.

The scale of the incident raises questions about how much trust businesses place in third-party website services. The affected organizations span several industries, including banking, technology, media, retail, and crypto.

HSBC was among the financial institutions affected, alongside Equifax and other major organizations. BBC, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, and Air France-KLM also appeared in Report URI’s investigation.

Ledger’s inclusion makes the incident particularly concerning for crypto users. The company is known for its hardware wallets, which help customers store private keys away from internet-connected devices. However, the incident demonstrates how threats can reach users through ordinary browsing activity, outside the hardware wallet itself.

The malicious campaign also contained capabilities targeting Apple devices. Researchers identified exploit infrastructure associated with Coruna and DarkSword, two iOS exploit kits designed to target vulnerabilities in iPhones and iPads.

This means the operation was not limited to stealing crypto or payment information. It also carried tools capable of targeting mobile devices through malicious webpage content.

Optimizely confirmed that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The company said it blocked access to the vulnerable pathway, deployed a fix, removed injected code, revoked active tokens, and reset access for affected accounts.

Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly. Updates: https://t.co/ptZHZviIeC

However, the incident raises serious questions about third-party website security. Report URI’s investigation found that even Optimizely’s own websites carried the malicious code. Researchers also observed the attacker rebuilding the malware 26 times during the campaign, adding capabilities and additional cryptocurrency wallets.

Most infected snippets were subsequently cleaned up, with Report URI finding only one remaining infected snippet in its final November 16 sweep.

But the financial damage and potential exposure remain difficult to measure. Researchers have identified crypto receipts, but the number of affected visitors, compromised payment cards, and exposed browser sessions remains unknown.

The bigger problem is that website visitors rarely know which third-party scripts are running behind the pages they trust. A familiar banking website, news outlet, or crypto platform can become an unexpected entry point for malicious code without its visitors noticing anything unusual.

#5449. Mindgruve Appoints Former WPP Executive Steve Terjeson as Vice President of Technology

Former Choreograph technology leader to accelerate AI innovation, advance Mindgruve's proprietary Sightline platform, and scale enterprise technology capabilities.

SAN DIEGO, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mindgruve, a modern media, commerce, and data technology company, today announced the appointment of Steve Terjeson as Vice President of Technology. Terjeson will lead Mindgruve's software development and data engineering teams, advancing the agency's established technology capabilities while accelerating innovation, scalability, and enterprise integration. A key priority will be driving the next generation of Sightline, Mindgruve's proprietary predictive marketing and business intelligence platform.

"Technology and data intelligence have long been central to how Mindgruve delivers measurable business growth for our clients," said Chad Robley, CEO of Mindgruve. "Sightline gives us a differentiated advantage that even the largest holding companies are working to replicate. Steve brings the enterprise technology experience to accelerate that advantage, scale our innovation, and deliver the sophistication of a global holding company with the agility and speed of an independent agency."

Terjeson joins Mindgruve from WPP's Choreograph, where he served as Vice President and acting CTO of data and technology for North America. He led enterprise data and technology delivery for global brands, managed a globally distributed engineering team, and developed sophisticated cloud data systems connecting brands' data to leading platforms, including Google and Adobe. He previously held senior roles at Wunderman Thompson (WPP), The Richards Group, and Costco Travel, with client experience spanning IBM, Uber, The Home Depot, and NBCUniversal.

"I've worked with marketing technology at nearly every scale throughout my career, and what Mindgruve has built stands alongside the very best," said Steve Terjeson, Vice President of Technology at Mindgruve. "The opportunity to build on an already sophisticated technology ecosystem, accelerate Sightline's evolution, and bring even more powerful AI and data-driven solutions to global brands is incredibly compelling. Mindgruve has the technology, talent, and entrepreneurial culture to move faster and deliver greater impact for clients."

In his new role, Terjeson will oversee Mindgruve's technology strategy and roadmap, with a focus on expanding the agency's AI, software engineering, cloud infrastructure, and data integration capabilities. He will also help accelerate the evolution of Sightline, strengthening its predictive intelligence, enterprise scalability, and ability to connect marketing investments directly to business outcomes. His leadership will further enhance the agency's commitment to delivering secure, flexible, and enterprise-grade technology solutions that enable smarter decisions, stronger marketing performance, and more profitable growth.

To learn how Mindgruve can turn your data into measurable growth, visit mindgruve.com/contact.

With over 750 experts worldwide, Mindgruve's teams deliver integrated media and commerce solutions for global brands.

#5448. Broker Action Coalition pushes for QM change on compensation cap

The Broker Action Coalition wants lender-paid broker compensation excluded from QM points and fees, aligning with retail LO pay. BAC says the current treatment harms small-balance and rural loans, citing 2026 wholesale data and prior CFPB findings.  AI Summary

The Broker Action Coalition (BAC) is proposing a change to federal mortgage rules that would exclude lender-paid mortgage broker compensation from the Qualified Mortgage (QM) points-and-fees calculation, aligning its treatment with compensation paid to retail lenders’ employee loan officers.

In a white paper recently released by BAC, the coalition argues that the current rules create an uneven playing field between independent mortgage brokers and retail lenders, particularly on smaller-balance loans.

Under the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule, points and fees generally cannot exceed 3% of a loan amount for loans of $137,958 or more in 2026. Smaller loans are subject to graduated percentage and dollar limits.

Currently, compensation paid by a wholesale lender to an independent mortgage broker counts toward that limit, while compensation paid by a retail lender to its own employee loan officer is excluded.

The coalition argues that both types of compensation are often funded through the interest rate and are indistinguishable from the borrower’s perspective. The difference can leave brokers with less room to cover other fees that count toward the cap, potentially causing otherwise qualifying loans to exceed the limit while losing QM status and its associated liability protections.

The disparity is particularly pronounced on smaller loans, where the dollar limits leave less room for additional charges. The coalition said small-balance and rural loans are particularly vulnerable because fixed-dollar charges consume a larger share of the available cap.

The white paper also points to a decline in small-dollar mortgage lending. The share of home purchase loans under $70,000 fell from more than 11% in 2011 to less than 4% in 2020, citing research from Pew Charitable Trusts, the Urban Institute and the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

In rural and lower-cost markets, the group argues, the restrictions can make it harder for brokers to compete for loans that are already less financially attractive to originate.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau‘s 2013 rulemaking established the distinction between employee and broker compensation. At the time, the bureau said including broker compensation in the calculation could help reduce the risk of mortgage brokers steering borrowers toward more expensive transactions.

The coalition acknowledges that consumer protection concern but argues that subsequent regulations addressing loan originator compensation and steering have made the points-and-fees restriction a less targeted way to address the issue.

Specifically, the group points to existing rules that prohibit loan originator compensation from varying based on a loan’s interest rate or other terms, as well as a separate prohibition on steering borrowers toward transactions that provide greater compensation.

The proposed reform would take two approaches: The primary proposal is a statutory amendment to the Truth in Lending Act that would exclude rate-funded creditor-to-broker compensation from the points-and-fees definition when it is paid under a compliant loan originator compensation agreement.

The parallel regulatory proposal would ask the CFPB to amend Regulation Z to create the same exclusion.

“The proposed reform would remove an inequitable regulatory constraint without changing the competitive forces that influence compensation today,” the paper reads. “While individual brokerages may adjust their compensation arrangements, there is little evidence to suggest that the reform would materially diminish the wholesale channel‘s overall pricing competitiveness.”

Under the proposed language, the exclusion would apply only when compensation is funded through the interest rate, is not paid directly by the borrower or financed into the loan amount, and is established through a standing agreement between the creditor and broker that does not vary based on individual loan terms.

The coalition said the proposed requirements would prevent brokers from adjusting compensation on individual loans to circumvent the cap. The change would leave the 3% limit and existing compensation and anti-steering rules intact, with borrower-paid compensation and other fees still subject to the cap.

Data from two wholesale lenders representing $13.4 billion in combined 2026 production showed that loans with 2.75% broker compensation accounted for 14.53% of units and 12.41% of volume. BAC said the figures indicate most brokered loans close with lower compensation.

The group also argued that the CFPB has authority under the Truth in Lending Act to make the change to preserve access to affordable mortgage credit. It cited the bureau’s 2019 assessment of the Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage rule, which documented fee waivers and other challenges affecting smaller brokered loans.

#5447. Coinbase plans to offer its own prediction market contracts in the first half of 2027

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Coinbase offers event contracts through a Kalshi partnership; own listings would give it more control over contracts and revenue

Coinbase Global is aiming to launch its own U.S. event contracts within the first six months of 2027, according to Bloomberg. Bloomberg, citing a person familiar with the matter, reports that both retail and institutional customers would be able to trade the contracts.

Coinbase now provides access to prediction markets by working with Kalshi. In-house contracts would let Coinbase decide which markets appear on its platform and retain a bigger share of trading revenue, according to Bloomberg.

A Coinbase spokesperson referred to the company's plans from October, when it said it would broaden its prediction-market offering and strengthen that business's economics by building its own clearing and other infrastructure. "We have nothing new to announce today," the spokesperson said, according to Bloomberg. The statement did not say when an in-house launch might happen.

In October, Chief Financial Officer Alesia Haas indicated that Coinbase intended to list a number of event contracts of its own, though she offered no timeline, according to Bloomberg. In the third quarter, annualized revenue from the event contracts business ran above $200 million.

In December 2025, Coinbase announced its acquisition of The Clearing Company, a startup focused on prediction markets, according to Bloomberg. The Clearing Company runs a regulated derivatives exchange, and in September the Commodity Futures Trading Commission signed off on a clearinghouse of its own.

Coinbase's prediction-market business faces legal pressure from state authorities. New York state has sued Coinbase, Kalshi and Gemini, arguing the platforms are unlawful gambling businesses. The platforms say they are federally regulated financial exchanges not subject to state betting laws.

New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin announced an investigation in August into the marketing practices of Polymarket, Kalshi, Coinbase and Gemini Titan. The CFTC holds primary oversight of platforms such as Kalshi and the U.S. arm of Polymarket.

#5445. AI inference servers shrink to fit the air-cooled racks enterprises already run

Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.

As AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

“Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija said. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.”

Botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. (* Disclosure below.)

Axelera’s Europa chip has been shipping since September. Ahead of SC26, the company unveiled Titania, a third-generation architecture that scales the design up to a 400-watt chip. The resulting six-kilowatt server is built to perform like leading data center GPUs while fitting into the existing 20- to 30-kilowatt air-cooled racks of an ordinary enterprise data center, Botija explained.

“Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre DPU is a pretty big deal,” he said. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.”

For enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the company’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage.

“Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija said. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your OPEX, and therefore be more profitable as a company.”

Stay tuned for the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of SC26.

(* Disclosure: NYSE Wired sponsored this segment of theCUBE. Neither NYSE Wired nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

#5444. Senate committee advances Matt Jones’ nomination as FHA commissioner

The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs voted 13-11 to advance Matt Jones’ nomination as HUD assistant secretary for housing and FHA commissioner, sending it to the full Senate.  AI Summary

Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote.

The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration. Jones would permanently fill the vacancy left by Frank Cassidy in June and succeed Joseph Gormley, who has been serving in the role on an acting basis.

Committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support. According to Scott, housing affordability remains one of the biggest challenges facing families across America, but if confirmed, Jones “will play an important role in implementing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and helping more families achieve the American dream of home ownership.”

Jones currently serves as HUD’s deputy assistant secretary for single-family housing. He previously was associate vice president of government housing finance at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), senior adviser for capital markets at Amerifirst Home Mortgage, and senior counsel for the Senate’s Finance and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs committees.The 13-11 vote reflected partisan divisions over the direction of federal housing policy and FHA’s role in addressing affordability and ownership gaps.

Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the committee’s ranking member, voted against the nomination, saying Jones’ office has “cut resources for first-time homebuyers and proposed weak rules for keeping foreclosed homes in the hands of families instead of corporations.”

“We should vote to make life more affordable for American families. But these nominees will do the opposite, accelerating the Trump administration‘s disastrous economic policies,” Warren said. If confirmed, Jones would oversee FHA’s single-family, multifamily and health care mortgage insurance portfolios. FHA currently insures roughly $2 trillion in mortgages.

The FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels. The results have renewed industry pressure on FHA to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums to ease costs for first-time and lower-income borrowers.

Jones would also inherit an agency that has seen a series of policy adjustments under HUD Secretary Scott Turner, including efforts to revise servicing standards and modernize technology infrastructure.

MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said the trade group supports the nomination due to Jones’ “extensive mortgage industry experience, deep understanding of government housing finance, and leadership of FHA’s single-family operations.”

“We urge the full Senate to confirm Matt Jones before the 119th Congress adjourns and look forward to working with him and HUD to continue modernizing FHA programs and to improve affordability for owning and renting a home,” Broeksmit said.

#5443. MemorialCare Neuroscience Institute First in Los Angeles and Orange Counties to Use Rapid Aneurysm Technology to Spot Hidden Brain Aneurysms

Rapid Aneurysm Technology Flags Suspected Aneurysms on CTA and MRA Brain Scans and Measures Them in 3D to Guide Monitoring and Treatment

FOUNTAIN VALLEY, Calif., Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MemorialCare Neuroscience Institute is advancing preventive brain aneurysm care across Southern California by detecting its first successful aneurysm before it ruptured using Rapid Aneurysm technology. Rapid Aneurysm is an artificial intelligence-powered technology, developed by RapidAI, that is embedded in all of MemorialCare's inpatient and outpatient qualifying brain CT angiography (CTA) and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) scans to automatically scan for potential aneurysms. It flags these suspected aneurysms for review by radiologists and neuro stroke teams and provides detailed three-dimensional measurements to help physicians determine the plan of care.

"One of the most important challenges in aneurysm care is determining which aneurysms require treatment and which can be monitored safely over time," said Viktor Szeder, M.D., neurointerventionalist, Division of Interventional Neuroradiology, MemorialCare Neuroscience Institute. "Finding an aneurysm before it ruptures gives us time to lower a patient's risk, watch for changes and, if needed, treat it in a planned procedure rather than an emergency. Rapid Aneurysm's precise measurements help us see subtle changes, so we know when monitoring is no longer enough."

According to the Brain Aneurysm Foundation, an estimated 6.8 million Americans are living with an unruptured brain aneurysm, many without symptoms. Because aneurysms can remain undetected until they rupture, early detection and ongoing monitoring are critical to reducing risk and determining when treatment may be necessary. Some aneurysms may be discovered unexpectedly when brain imaging is performed for another medical reason.

"Rapid Aneurysm analyzes CTA and MRA brain scans to automatically flag suspected aneurysms," said Dr. Szeder. "Traditionally, physicians measure an aneurysm by hand on flat, two-dimensional images, recording its height and width. Because many aneurysms are small and irregularly shaped, slight growth can be difficult to measure consistently from one scan to the next."

Rapid Aneurysm converts those images into detailed three-dimensional models that measure the aneurysm's full volume and surface area, then compares them across scans to show whether it is growing or changing shape. Growth is one of the key factors physicians weigh when deciding between continued monitoring and treatment, as aneurysms that grow are significantly more likely to rupture than those that remain stable.

Patients do not need a separate scan or appointment for the AI analysis; it is automatically created in the workflow for any MemorialCare patient who receives a CTA or MRA. Radiologists confirm every diagnosis, and patients with a confirmed aneurysm are connected with MemorialCare Neuroscience Institute specialists for follow-up care.

"At MemorialCare, we believe better health starts with prevention and finding risks early," said Liz Acord, vice president of clinical institutes, MemorialCare. "Rapid Aneurysm gives us the opportunity to be proactive rather than reactive. Bringing this technology to all MemorialCare's patients from the South Bay to South Orange County strengthens our commitment to the health of the communities we serve."

MemorialCare Neuroscience Institute provides neurovascular care at Long Beach Medical Center, Orange Coast Medical Center and Saddleback Medical Center. Long Beach Medical Center is home to a Comprehensive Stroke Center and the Division of Interventional Neuroradiology, which has provided minimally invasive treatment for brain aneurysms, vascular malformations and stroke for 15 years. Its interventional neuroradiologists and stroke neurologists are available 24 hours a day for consultation and emergency treatment.

Learn more about Rapid Aneurysm at memorialcare.org/RapidAI.

MemorialCare's clinical networks include the MemorialCare Orthopedic & Spine Institute, MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute, MemorialCare Cancer Institute, MemorialCare Neuroscience Institute and MemorialCare Research Program. MemorialCare operates Select Health Plan and provides primary, urgent, and outpatient care through MemorialCare Medical Group and MemorialCare Independent Physicians (IPA). It also offers the subscription-free "Get Care Now" virtual care suite. #5442. Trump says U.S. might allow Nvidia AI chip sales to China in two to three years

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Trump said Blackwell chips will be obsolete in a year, while a bill in Congress would bar their sale to China for at least 18 months

President Donald Trump said the U.S. could allow Nvidia $NVDA to sell its Blackwell AI chips to China in two to three years, once newer processors supersede them.

“In two years or three years, I would, if I were here, I would say, go ahead,” Trump said in an interview with Bloomberg during his trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Trump’s term ends in January 2029.

He said Nvidia is working on chips that will replace Blackwell. "In another year, they'll be obsolete," Trump said of the Blackwell line. He called the H200 processors the U.S. allowed Nvidia to sell to China "semi-obsolete" and said, "the 200s are old now."

Nvidia lobbied the U.S. government under Jensen Huang for permission to sell Blackwell chips to China, according to Bloomberg. The Trump administration never granted that request and approved sales of the less advanced H200 instead.

Some U.S. lawmakers want Congress to block Blackwell sales to China for at least 18 months, according to Bloomberg. Sen. Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, have steered their AI Overwatch Act to the last stage of talks on the yearly defense bill.

Nvidia stopped shipping licensed Hopper data center chips to China, interim CEO Colette Kress said on an earnings call on Tuesday. The Hopper family includes the H200. Nvidia booked $2.4 billion in China sales of licensed Hopper hardware in its fiscal third quarter, which ended Oct. 25. Kress gave no reason for the halt.

The halt came days after Huang, Nvidia's co-founder, resigned as CEO on Nov. 12 after admitting to an affair. The woman is a former executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer based in Singapore. U.S. intelligence officials suspect she is an agent of Beijing's spy agencies. China's Foreign Ministry has called the espionage allegation unsubstantiated.

The Trump administration also issued rules that limit sales of advanced U.S. chips to data centers that plan to give Chinese companies remote access. Kress said Nvidia's backlog of unfilled orders for high-end products such as Vera Rubin means the rules would not affect its top-line revenue.

#5441. Before You Raise the Camera, Listen: A Photographer's Case for Slowing Down and Using All Five Senses

Brand strategist Jeff Stern, whose career spans P&G and Hershey, introduces the Five-Sense Lens in A Change of Scenery, now available from Palmetto Publishing.

CHARLESTON, S.C., Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Palmetto Publishing has released A Change of Scenery, a travel memoir and photography collection by Jeff Stern. The book traces a journey through all seven continents, beginning with a solo trip to the American Southwest in March 2020 after a photography conference was cancelled and much of the world stopped moving.

Stern structures the book continent by continent. Each photograph appears alongside the full sensory record of the moment it was made. Readers encounter the smoky, fermented taste of kymyz offered inside a Kyrgyz yurt, frost crystals falling as a tent unzips on the Sary-Jaz Mountains at sunrise, and robusta coffee two hours after dawn in the rice paddies of Northwest Vietnam. At White Pocket in Arizona, standing on rock that pulsed terracotta and ochre beneath a cobalt sky, Stern made himself a promise about the role creative expression would play in the rest of his life.

The book's central tension is one of self-definition. Stern resists the label of landscape photographer, describing it as a box that felt polished, precise, and oddly impersonal. He calls himself a scenery enthusiast instead, arguing that scenery is not a view but a sensory event. That renaming required him to set aside the technical measures by which photographers are usually judged and to trust a creative voice he spent much of his life believing he did not have.

Jeff Stern stated, "I kept asking myself the same questions after every scene, and none of them were about aperture or shutter speed. They were: What did I hear? What did the ground feel like underfoot? I wrote this book because those questions changed what I was able to see, and I think they can do the same for anyone who spends time in nature â with or without a camera."

The book closes with the Five-Sense Lens, a framework Stern built from those recurring questions. Readers can try an interactive version of the Five-Sense Lens at https://sceneryenthusiast.com.

A Change of Scenery is positioned for 3 types of readers:

It arrives as interest in slow travel and attention-based creative practice continues to grow, and as many readers reconsider trips postponed or reimagined during the period in which the book opens. Palmetto Publishing lists the title under biography and autobiography for artists, architects, and photographers.

Stern holds an MBA from Dartmouth's Tuck School of Business and a BS in Marketing from California State University. He built and led brands at Procter & Gamble, The Hershey Company, Brown-Forman, and Humana before turning to consulting, where he has spent the past nine years as a partner at The Partnering Group, a firm serving consumer goods and retail companies.

A Change of Scenery is available for purchase online at Amazon.com and BarnesandNoble.com. A limited Collector's Edition is available at https://sceneryenthusiast.com. For more information about the author, please visit any of his social media platforms.

#5438. What we learned from Nvidia’s first earnings call without Jensen Huang

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The company made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress said the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the company held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress announced plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

For information technology buyers, nothing changes about what you’ve ordered or planned over the next 18 to 24 months. Don’t pause a deployment because of a leadership headline. The advice I gave in August still applies: Welcome Nvidia’s simplification and hedge the dependency.

One of the more interesting comments on the call came from Jones, not Kress. In describing the CEO search, which will consider both internal and external candidates, he said the board “appreciates that we’re living in a world where advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are driving major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will need to navigate those waters carefully.”

That was paired with immediate action. On the morning of earnings, the board created a standing national security and export control oversight committee of three directors that will retain outside experts. Kress disclosed that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China and noted that the U.S. Commerce Department issued new export controls this week, which the company “still has some time to study.”

Huang was a product visionary who also served as the industry’s chief diplomat. The board is now signaling that fluency in Washington is a core requirement, on par with technical vision.

For IT leaders at multinationals, export policy is now a deployment variable. The new Commerce rule is intended to block remote access to advanced chips via data centers in third countries, so the location of your capacity and who can access it are now compliance questions. Bring your compliance team into AI infrastructure planning early.

With demand still far ahead of supply, who gets Nvidia systems matters more than what they cost. Kress laid out the criteria more clearly than I’ve heard before. First are land, power and shell, meaning whether a customer’s facility is ready to receive and use the gear in the quarter it ships. Second is capital. Third, for customers that aren’t investment-grade, is proof of off-take, or evidence that someone has committed to use the capacity.

“All are getting the same pricing,” Kress said. “That is super important for us, and we just need to assure that they are ready on their side in terms of being able to accept the compute.”

Those same factors were incorporated into the guidance. Kress said the outlook “considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The reality is that the AI bottleneck has shifted from the chip to the building, the grid and the balance sheet. Nvidia is serving as the industry’s underwriter, determining who is ready.

The lesson for enterprise buyers is that readiness is the currency. If you want on-premises systems, secure power, cooling and funding before requesting allocation. If you can’t, buy capacity from a provider that has already cleared this hurdle. In my view, this also helps explain why sovereign AI is growing so quickly for Nvidia. Those projects often arrive with land and power already in place.

Over the past year, Nvidia has used its balance sheet to seed the ecosystem through guarantees, investments, and commitments to neoclouds and AI labs. Though  neoclouds remain important, Kress brought a different tone to this audience. She said Nvidia will “continue to be disciplined and selective” in supporting neoclouds and that it is “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees” as other sources of capital become available. Asked about vendor financing, she acknowledged that “a lot of things have changed over this last quarter.”

Two notable details emerged during the call. When Bernstein Research analyst Stacy Rasgon pressed on what he read as new disclosure language about neocloud commitments, Kress explained that Nvidia’s guarantees take effect only after a partner has raised its own debt and equity, built the facility and installed the compute. If the project stalls, the guarantee lapses.

“Is it new? No. Did we change anything? No,” she said. Even so, spelling it out clarifies Nvidia’s participation in neoclouds. When asked about uses of capital beyond the share buyback, which she said Nvidia still plans to complete, she put suppliers first: “The top priority is going to be our suppliers.” Prepayments to expand capacity come before customer financing, which will be reserved for “very strong customers.”

This was a critical piece of information for investors. I’ve previously compared vendor-financed neoclouds to the CLECs of the internet era, where the financing organization was left holding the bag. A CFO-led Nvidia appears to see the same risk. The result is a shakeout in which well-capitalized neoclouds with contracted demand grow stronger, while thinly funded ones struggle to secure systems. This should offer some comfort to investors that circular financing has been de-risked.

The flip side is that someone still must fund the buildout outside the hyperscalers. Kress pointed to infrastructure capital partners establishing financing platforms. Whether that money arrives as fast as Nvidia steps back is what to watch for.

My advice to IT buyers is to ask, before signing a multiyear deal with a neocloud, how it’s financed, how much capacity is committed and where it stands in Nvidia’s allocation queue. Those were niche questions a year ago. They should be standard due diligence now.

The demand story has shifted from training models to running agents, broadening what customers need from Nvidia. Citing OpenRouter data, Kress said agentic workloads now account for roughly 80% of tokens. Falling token prices are driving more usage, keeping GPU rental rates climbing.

The CPU growth story shouldn’t surprise anyone. In May, I wrote that agentic AI opens a massive new spigot for Nvidia on the CPU side. This quarter, demand outpaced supply. “Agentic AI is driving extraordinary demand for CPUs, far outstripping supply,” Kress said, noting that Nvidia’s Vera CPU is now adopted by CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and Open AI. Agents spend much of their time calling tools, running code and moving data, which is general-purpose work. A CPU shortage amid a GPU boom shows how quickly the workload is changing.

Nvidia is also filling in the layers above and around the hardware. The agent safety platform pairs OpenShell, which limits what agents can access, with Sentry, which runs on BlueField data processing units and monitors agent behavior in silicon. In my view, the biggest barrier to deploying agents in production is control, not model quality.

The network is part of this, too. Kress said co-packaged optics is in volume production, and Lambda’s deployment, announced at this week’s SC26 conference, is the first large-scale proof point. Nvidia is a formidable networking vendor, though buyers mixing accelerators will still want to weigh a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing chip.

For IT buyers, plan CPU capacity for agent workloads now, and insist that agent controls reside outside the model, in infrastructure you can audit.

The question of who the new CEO will be might not be just about Nvidia but about the entire industry. If the board goes internal, Ian Buck seems to be the frontrunner. Externally, the names most bandied about are Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su, Arm Ltd. CEO Rene Haas and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian, or we could see Manuvir Das make a comeback and return to the company.

Most industry watchers describe Nvidia as a chip company, a view that is about a decade out of date. Nvidia’s value comes from the full systems it has built around its silicon. Each is a stack tailored to an industry: hardware, libraries, frameworks, pretrained models, simulation and developer tools, all tuned to work together.

The next CEO must treat silicon as a key layer of an open, secure, agentic enterprise stack. Enterprises won’t buy GPUs. They’ll buy outcomes: agents that run safely on governed data across clouds, on-premises and at the edge. Whoever runs Nvidia next must sell that outcome, play well within an ecosystem Nvidia doesn’t fully control, and make security a core part of the platform. Here are three dark-horse candidates to consider:

Matt Garman. The Amazon Web Services Inc. CEO has led the world’s largest cloud through the shift to AI. He knows what it takes to turn infrastructure into consumable services at enormous scale. Garman also lives the open-stack approach: AWS offers model choice, runs its own Trainium chips alongside Nvidia’s, and sells to enterprises that want flexibility rather than lock-in. He would bring operational discipline and a deep feel for the customer. The question is whether Nvidia’s biggest customer-turned-competitor can credibly lead the supplier.

Jeetu Patel, Cisco Systems Inc.’s president and chief product officer, is the best storyteller in enterprise tech after Huang himself. He has spent the past few years rebuilding Cisco’s portfolio around secure AI infrastructure, integrating networking, security and observability into a single platform. That is exactly the “open, secure, agentic” stack Nvidia must deliver. Patel thinks in platforms, moves quickly,and has been personally using AI agents to shape his product views. He also has deep enterprise credibility, which Nvidia needs more than additional credibility with hyperscalers.

Charlie Giancarlo, CEO of Everpure (formerly Pure Storage), may be the most underrated name here. He built networking businesses at Cisco, spent time in private equity, and has repositioned Pure as a data management company. Storage revenue is growing thanks to hyperscaler wins. Giancarlo understands that agentic AI depends on data and that the data layer and the network are where enterprise AI succeeds or fails. He is a systems thinker who has led a platform transition before.

Two final points on the CEO hire: For some reason, there is a tremendous amount of industry chatter that Jensen Huang was the only person at Nvidia with key relationships with suppliers, partners, and other ecosystem providers. I know for a fact that is not true. Nvidia’s leadership, which includes Buck, Deb Shoquist (executive vice president of operations), Nico Caprez (vice president of global AI development), Gilad Shainer and Kevin Deierling (networking leadership), Kress and others, all have deep relationships with the ecosystem.

Also, I wouldn’t expect the board to make a snap decision about its next CEO. The roadmap is baked beyond Feynman, and the company can continue for a couple of years, if needed. This is an important hire; the board should take its time and ensure it’s the right person.

This call confirmed what many industry watchers, including me, have long believed: The moat was built in layers, and those layers held. Supply is constrained, the roadmap is set and customers are still asking for more than Nvidia can build.

Kress closed the call by saying, “We’ve got this.” On execution, I believe her. Kress is a steady hand right now, and the discipline she brings to capital allocation should make the AI buildout healthier. The bets that created Nvidia’s position, though, were placed years before the market arrived. Post-Jensen, Nvidia will continue to perform as it did; as Robbins put it, no one is bigger than the industry.

My advice to IT buyers is to stick with current plans and closely monitor the CEO search. Since Nvidia’s roadmap is baked through Feynman and beyond, it can ride momentum for the next two years or longer.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5437. E.U. plans to revamp oil reserve rules to match emergency stocks to national fuel use

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A draft document would require at least one third of emergency stocks to be held as products other than crude oil

The European Commission is preparing to overhaul E.U. oil stockpiling rules so the product mix in emergency stocks reflects each member state's fuel use, according to Bloomberg. A draft document seen by Bloomberg on Thursday lays out the plan, which the Commission intends to approve in early December, though the text may change.

Current rules do not oblige countries to align the kinds of fuel they hold in reserve with what they actually burn at home, according to Bloomberg. Under the draft, stock composition would need to feature a minimum of one refined product, with options including fuel oil, diesel, jet fuel and gasoline. The draft would also let armed forces tap emergency liquid fuel reserves on a temporary, exceptional basis, provided certain requirements are met.

The draft says: "At least one third of emergency stocks must be held as products other than crude oil, and composition should reflect the national risk assessment, including refining capacity and domestic needs," according to Bloomberg. The Commission declined to comment, Bloomberg said.

The Commission said in an April communication that it would begin revising the Oil Stocks Directive to address weaknesses identified in the current crisis. It said it would consider whether different oil products need specific stock requirements. The document said about 40% of E.U. jet fuel consumption is imported and about half of those imports pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

The Middle East conflict added €40 billion ($44 billion) to the E.U.'s spending on imported diesel and between €16 billion and €19 billion to its jet fuel costs from March through September, according to Bloomberg, citing E.U. estimates. The same estimates put the cost of a one-week interruption to fuel supplies at 0.15% to 0.2% of the average member state's yearly GDP. Oil accounts for about 38% of E.U. energy consumption.

European governments have been releasing reserves to ease prices. French Economy Minister Roland Lescure said on Oct. 29 that Europe would put 42 million barrels of its oil reserves on the market over three months, with half of the volume in diesel. Lescure said at the time that Europe would leave open the possibility of additional releases.
