#5435. Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm

Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

#5434. Sanofi is weighing a takeover bid for U.S. respiratory drugmaker Insmed

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Insmed stock rose as much as 24% on Thursday, and any deal could be weeks away, according to Bloomberg

Sanofi is considering a purchase of U.S. respiratory drugmaker Insmed and is in talks with advisers about a possible transaction, according to Bloomberg.

Deliberations remain under way, a deal could take weeks to materialize, and rival suitors might yet surface, according to Bloomberg. Sanofi said its policy is to stay silent on speculation circulating in the market, according to Reuters. Representatives for Insmed declined to comment, according to Bloomberg.

Insmed stock jumped by up to 24% during Thursday's session and was trading 20% higher as of 11:44 a.m. in New York, which put the company's worth at $31.6 billion. Sanofi stock ended the Paris session roughly 2.9% lower, leaving the company valued at about €101 billion ($111 billion).

If a deal is struck, it could become the biggest transaction the worldwide biopharma industry has seen since Pfizer $PFE acquired Seagen $SGEN in a $43 billion purchase at the end of 2023, according to Bloomberg.

Bridgewater, New Jersey-based Insmed has two approved respiratory drugs: Brinsupri, which treats non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis, and Arikayce, which treats refractory mycobacterium avium complex lung disease. Insmed said third-quarter revenue rose 268% from a year earlier to $524.4 million.

Sanofi CEO Belén Garijo said during last month's earnings call that the company planned to lean on dealmaking to help drive its expansion, according to Bloomberg. Chief Financial Officer François-Xavier Roger told reporters on a call that "the amount at stake is bigger than what we sought in the past," according to Bloomberg.

Sanofi expanded its immunology alliance with Regeneron $REGN in October, under which Regeneron will receive $1 billion upfront and be eligible for up to $7 billion in milestone payments. Dupixent, the drug at the center of that alliance, is expected to begin losing patent protection in the early 2030s.

In July, Sanofi ended development of amlitelimab in atopic dermatitis after a series of late-stage setbacks. The decision came after Garijo replaced Paul Hudson as chief executive.

#5433. What Is Backpack Crypto? BP Explodes 30% After CFTC Approval

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

First, what is Backpack crypto? Why is it exploding? Backpack is suddenly becoming one of the market’s hottest stories after securing a major regulatory breakthrough in the United States. Its native BP token surged 30% in 24 hours as traders rushed to price in the exchange’s latest expansion. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has effectively opened the door for Backpack to challenge established crypto derivatives platforms on American soil.

The approval gives Backpack the regulatory foundation to operate a US derivatives exchange and clearinghouse. Its ambitions extend beyond simply offering another place to trade Bitcoin and Ethereum. The company wants to combine leveraged crypto trading, collateral management, and global liquidity under one regulated platform.

The development also arrives as competition heats up over who can deliver the next generation of crypto trading infrastructure.

Founded by Armani Ferrante, Backpack started as a Solana-focused crypto wallet and exchange. It has since expanded into securities, tokenization, and derivatives. The company then reports more than $450 billion in cumulative trading volume and customers across over 150 countries.

Its latest breakthrough involves two separate approvals from the CFTC. The Designated Contract Market (DCM) registration allows Backpack to operate a regulated derivatives exchange.

Backpack is coming home to the USA. 🇺🇸We’ve received landmark CFTC approval to establish the first-ever derivatives exchange powered by one order book with unified global liquidity.Leveraged perpetuals. Crypto collateral. Cross-margin. 24/7 trading.Join the waitlist:…

Meanwhile, its Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO) registration provides the infrastructure needed to manage collateral, margin, and settlement obligations. Together, these approvals establish the foundation for Backpack to offer leveraged crypto perpetual futures in the United States.

The proposed platform will support 24/7 trading, crypto and fiat collateral, cross-margining, and access to Backpack’s global order book.

That last feature could prove particularly important. Rather than isolating American traders inside a separate liquidity pool, Backpack wants to connect US customers with its international trading ecosystem.

BP responded immediately. The token climbed by more than 30% over 24 hours to $1.10, pushing its market cap higher as trading activity accelerated. The rally ties to growing expectations that Backpack could become a serious competitor in the American derivatives market.

The regulatory breakthrough also strengthens its position against offshore platforms that have dominated leveraged crypto trading for years.

Backpack’s approval exposes an interesting opportunity across the wider crypto market. Bitcoin remains the industry’s largest liquidity pool, yet its base layer was never designed for sophisticated smart contracts, high-speed decentralized trading or complex margin products.

That creates an infrastructure gap developers are racing to fill. Solana demonstrated how quickly decentralized applications can execute transactions. Bitcoin, meanwhile, offers a much deeper pool of established capital.

Bringing those strengths together could unlock an entirely different market for Bitcoin-denominated trading.

Projects exploring this direction, Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER), which combines Bitcoin Layer 2 infrastructure with Solana Virtual Machine technology. Its architecture aims to let users bridge BTC into a faster environment supporting smart contracts and decentralized applications.

The potential goes beyond faster transfers. Bitcoin liquidity could eventually support decentralized spot markets, margin trading, and perpetual futures without forcing traders to abandon Bitcoin for another blockchain ecosystem.

Bitcoin Hyper has already attracted more than $33.2 million through its presale, exceeding Backpack’s previously disclosed $17 million Series A funding round. Its token currently sells for just $0.0137, while its staking program advertises rewards of up to 35% APY.

With its November 26 launch target approaching, the presale is entering its final stretch. The combination of Bitcoin liquidity and Solana-style execution is attracting attention as developers look for ways to bring more sophisticated financial applications to Bitcoin.

Backpack now has something many offshore competitors cannot easily replicate: a regulatory pathway into the American derivatives market. The company still needs to turn its approvals into actual trading activity, but the potential market is enormous.

American traders represent an important source of institutional and retail liquidity. Bringing them into a unified order book could strengthen Backpack’s competitive position while attracting market makers and professional trading firms.

BP’s 30% rally shows investors are already anticipating that expansion, and Backpack’s regulatory breakthrough could mark the beginning of a much larger shift in crypto trading.

The race is no longer just about building another exchange. It is about connecting deeper liquidity, faster execution, and increasingly sophisticated financial products. Bitcoin’s enormous capital base makes that opportunity particularly difficult to ignore.

#5431. Crypto platform’s plan to offer tokenized shares for Anthropic IPO comes up short, following similar SpaceX flop

In the lead up to Anthropic’s record-setting Thursday IPO, several crypto platforms announced plans to offer their customers exposure to the offering in the form of tokens tied to its shares. It’s far from clear, however, whether these tokenized stocks—crypto tokens designed to track a stock’s price—will actually provide exposure at Anthropic’s offering price, or at all. The maker of the Claude chatbot opened at $111.50 a share on Nasdaq, about 34% above its $83 IPO price.

Binance Wallet, the wallet tied to the crypto exchange, is already off to a rocky start. Minutes after the stock began trading, the platform said it hadn’t secured enough shares to fill customers’ orders. It said it would refund everyone who put up money and split the available tokens among eligible customers for free, based on how much each had committed.

The announcement came a day after Binanced Wallet opened Anthropic-linked tokens at the company’s eventual IPO price, plus a 5% fee. Within hours, users had committed $500 million, hitting the campaign’s cap and prompting it to close early. Firms like Binance typically offer tokenized stocks by obtaining allocations of shares for themselves, which they hold in custody, and then issue tokens that serve as claims on the stock.

Kraken also let eligible customers request Anthropic-linked tokens at the final IPO price plus 5%, without guaranteeing an allocation. Ondo, a tokenization platform, took a different approach. It said it would launch its token once Anthropic shares began trading on Nasdaq, giving buyers exposure at market prices rather than a shot at the IPO price. Other platforms, including Bitget and bStocks, also joined the rush.

Tokenized stocks have gained momentum over the past year as crypto companies have used them to bring U.S. equities to investors abroad. They let buyers gain exposure to those stocks without owning shares directly and, on some platforms, trade outside regular market hours. That growth is part of a broader push to put traditional assets on blockchains. By September, the total value of tokenized real-world assets had topped $34 billion, according to a report by blockchain analytics platform Dune. Tokenized stocks grew fastest, rising more than 2,000% as the number of active holders surpassed 1 million.

In an IPO, tokenized stocks can give buyers who might otherwise have to wait for public trading a chance to get in at the offering price. That can be a better deal if the stock opens higher, but it depends on whether the token provider secures enough shares to fill their orders.

SpaceX’s IPO in June was an early stress test for tokenized IPO access, and several crypto platforms came up short. The company priced its IPO at $135 a share, with investors requesting more than four times as many shares as were on offer.

The surge in demand left token providers scrambling for shares. Binance Wallet, for example, had taken requests from customers hoping to buy in at the IPO price, but its token provider couldn’t secure enough shares to fill those orders. Binance Wallet canceled the offering and refunded customers, who missed out on the opening jump when SpaceX began trading about 11% above its IPO price.

#5430. Want to build an AI operating model? First, build consensus

Joanne Wright is Senior Vice President, Transformation and Operations, at IBM. Yogi Goyal is IBM Consulting's Global and Americas Managing Partner for its Business Orchestration services. IBM hosted a Fortune COO dinner.

At a recent dinner with chief operating officers in New York City, we caught up with the senior leaders most often tasked with transforming AI use into value. The conversation was markedly different from the ones we were having just one year ago.

In 2025, peers in the C-suite would boast about individual AI successes: An agent that made software engineers more productive, or an AI use case in accounting that dethroned the spreadsheet.

But this year, conversations were focused on the forest, not the trees. Individual successes felt insufficient. The bigger question was: How do you do this again and again? How do you build a foundation that makes AI success second nature?

Leaders want an AI Operating Model: an enterprise-wide foundation that makes agents, automation, and intelligent data routine. Because the alternative is exhausting: fighting tooth and nail to scale individual AI projects.

Unfortunately, exhaustion is the status quo.

Why? One reason is a misconception about who builds the AI Operating Model. Ask who owns AI, and every executive raises a hand: the CIO for the technology, the CAIO for the models, the CFO for the investment, the CHRO for the workforce.

In reality, it’s a joint effort across the C-suite. Still, someone must steward these efforts. Often that’s the COO, whose remit spans every function. But even the COO can’t make executive decisions across every business unit. Instead, they need to build consensus. And so a decidedly old-school skill – influence – is at the center of AI success today. Rolling up your sleeves and building relationships, not AI models, is what matters most.

Let’s start with the AI Operating Model. What is it, exactly? An AI Operating Model is a reusable foundation underneath all your individual AI investments. At its core, the operating model connects four key areas. First is intelligence: trusted, real-time context that lets agents make smart decisions. The second is action: The ability for that intelligence to span the enterprise, from people and workflows to applications and APIs. Then comes operations – the ability to observe and optimize that action across the business. And finally, control: Ensuring AI has rigorous governance and security.

Intelligence, action, operations, and control span front- and back-office functions. They touch technical and non-technical roles. They involve employees at all levels. This is where consensus building comes in. Being able to shape decisions, rather than execute them with complete authority, can be more valuable. The real work is building consensus into how the enterprise runs, so it holds from one initiative to the next.

When we sit down with clients, that last step is where we see most companies stall. Leaders agree on the vision, then each function goes off and builds its own AI, and the agreement never makes it into the work. The technology is ready: Taking a company’s standard operating procedures and turning them into agentic use cases, an ROI case, and a blueprint used to take days or weeks. Now it can take hours. The hard part is agreeing on what to build. The symptoms show up in three places. On value, CEOs report that only 25% of AI initiatives have delivered expected ROI over the last few years. On workflows, 82% of C-suite executives say functional silos block value. On platforms, half of CEOs say the pace of recent investments has left their organization with disconnected, piecemeal technology. Closing those gaps takes consensus.

We didn’t get this right at IBM from the start. Our early wins came quickly, as they do for most companies. What has let us keep scaling was consensus. We now apply the same practices with clients, and start by asking a few simple questions:

Today’s AI leaders must be savvy technologists, but that’s not enough. They also need the necessary credibility, communication, and consensus-building skills. The most impactful AI leaders excel when they surface evidence to shape decisions about AI investments.

Today’s AI leaders must be savvy technologists, but that’s not enough. They also need the necessary credibility, communication, and consensus-building skills. According to IBM’s new Chief AI Officer Study, the most impactful AI leaders excel when they surface evidence to shape AI investment decisions.

If AI leaders can’t do this, they’ll launch one-off AI projects and chase ROI. But if AI leaders can get peers on the same page about an AI Operating Model, they’ll build an AI value creation flywheel. One where productivity fuels investment, and investment fuels greater growth.

#5429. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5428. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping — release date, cast and plot explained

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Sunrise on the Reaping opens Nov. 20, 2026. See 10 characters, who plays them and the casting bet behind each role.

The people making the next Hunger Games film don't have to find an audience. They have to avoid disappointing the one already waiting for it. That audience is large, and it comes from two directions. Moviegoers have followed the franchise through five films, Variety reports, and readers bought 1.5 million copies of the new novel in its first week, according to TheWrap. The novel came out in 2025, according to ABC News, and its readers will reach the theater with the story still fresh. Sunrise on the Reaping faces a double test, with readers holding it up against the novel and moviegoers holding it up against the earlier performances in these roles.

Many characters in the film are people fans have already met, now younger and played by someone else, and each of those casting choices invites a comparison before filming even begins. The setting makes those comparisons unavoidable. The story goes back to the 50th Hunger Games, the Second Quarter Quell, according to Collider. At an earlier Games, known figures have to appear at an earlier stage of their lives rather than as new creations. The producers have met that pressure by putting experienced, well-known actors even in supporting parts. "We've been blessed with very sophisticated actors in our roles," Nina Jacobson, a producer at Color Force, told Variety. The story still belongs to a lead most viewers have never seen before, and the stars around him are there to steady the film rather than to take it over.

Rotten Tomatoes set out to introduce the film's major characters and the actors playing them, from Glenn Close's Drusilla Sickle and Kieran Culkin's Caesar Flickerman to a young Plutarch Heavensbee. Taken together, these casting choices amount to a series of bets, each on whether a new actor can make an old character feel both familiar and new. Audiences can start judging those bets when the film opens in U.S. theaters on Nov. 20, 2026, according to . Each character below represents one of those bets. Some depend on keeping a known figure recognizable, some on rebuilding one, and some on a star in a part that looks small on paper. For each, the thing to watch is whether viewers stop comparing and accept the person on screen.

Sunrise on the Reaping depends on a character fans think they know well, played by an actor few of them know at all. Haymitch is the film's main character, according to Variety, and Rotten Tomatoes reports that Joseph Zada plays the young Haymitch and leads the cast. Zada has no famous name to draw a crowd. His earlier credits include We Were Liars, and ABC News reports that the Sydney-born actor also appeared in the Australian series The Invisible Boys and Total Control. The well-known actors around him can give the film stature, but only Zada's performance can make its central character work.

Audiences will compare this Haymitch with the older one Woody Harrelson played in the original films. Zada follows an actor who has earned three Oscar nominations, according to ABC News, and that is a demanding standard for a newcomer. The film's director, Francis Lawrence, acknowledges that following Harrelson in the role is a heavy task, according to The Associated Press. A copy of Harrelson's performance would only invite the comparison, and Zada has to build the role anew.

Zada plays Haymitch as the opposite of the man fans remember. The character is 16 in this story, according to Parade, and Zada chose to show the boy before the damage. "He's a heartbreaking character so the best job that I could do was to make him loving and caring, so we can see how much this person has been through to reach the cynical, alcoholic, sarcastic person that is Woody's Haymitch," Zada told ABC News. Haymitch is one of 48 tributes reaped for the 50th Games, double the usual number, according to ABC News. A contest that large and that cruel makes it believable that a caring boy comes out of it broken.

If Zada succeeds, viewers will see Harrelson's drunk as a survivor rather than a joke, and they will understand a character they thought they already knew in a new way.

Fans have already watched President Coriolanus Snow at two very different points in his life, and the actor who takes over the role has to answer to both. Most viewers picture the older Snow, the ruler Donald Sutherland played in all four original films, according to Variety. The younger Snow is a recent memory, because Tom Blyth played him in 2023’s The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. Ralph Fiennes plays Snow in Sunrise on the Reaping, Rotten Tomatoes reports, and his performance has to make one man of the young Snow viewers saw and the old Snow they remember.

Most recasting aims to make a character new, but this casting aims to keep Snow recognizable. "We wanted to honor Donald Sutherland by having one of this generation's greatest actors play President Snow 24 years before Katniss Everdeen entered the arena," Nina Jacobson, a producer at Color Force, told Variety. The Snow in this film already holds power, and Fiennes has to play him in a way that points ahead to the man Sutherland played. That sets an unusual standard for success. Fiennes succeeds if viewers can see Sutherland's Snow taking shape in him, not if he makes the character entirely his own.

Fiennes’s recent work backs up the producer’s praise. His performance in Conclave earned him Academy Award and Golden Globe nominations, according to Variety. His Harry Potter role also means he has already played a major part in a long-running franchise.

With Snow, the film uses star power to serve continuity. Audiences will watch a third actor in the role, and the casting works if they still recognize the president Sutherland played.

On paper, Drusilla Sickle is defined by a job rather than a story. Rotten Tomatoes lists her as the escort for District 12, the Capitol official who accompanies that district's tributes, which is a part most viewers would expect to stay at the edge of the frame. The filmmakers gave that supporting post to Glenn Close, who has earned eight Oscar nominations, according to Variety. The distance between the size of the role and the stature of the actor is the bet. The filmmakers are wagering that a performer with her record can turn a chaperone into someone audiences remember after the credits roll.

The producers expect Close to make a minor part into a defining one. "Glenn Close is a dream Drusilla. She brings so much of her intellect and imagination to each role, creating characters who are unforgettable and iconic," producer Nina Jacobson told Variety. An iconic escort is a large ambition, and it reaches beyond Close's own scenes. Drusilla represents the Capitol to District 12's tributes up close, so the way Close plays her will shape how viewers read the Capitol's treatment of the young people it sends into the arena. A warm Drusilla, a cold one or a careless one would each tell the audience something different about the people who run the Games.

Close's casting pays off if she makes the Capitol's chaperone feel essential to the story, and it falls short if a star of her standing ends up with too little to do.

The film has given one of its backstage Capitol jobs to a star. Magno Stift is the fashion designer for the tributes, according to Rotten Tomatoes, and Billy Porter, whom many viewers know from Pose, plays him. TheWrap reports that Magno is District 12's designer, a working post rather than a seat of power. A job like that rarely draws much attention on its own, so Magno is a clear test of the decision to put famous actors in small parts. If audiences take to the character, much of the credit will belong to Porter and to the people who cast him.

Magno's marriage explains why the part needed a big name. He is the estranged husband of Drusilla Sickle, TheWrap reports, so he works alongside the tributes while living with a broken marriage to another member of the Capitol staff. Glenn Close plays Drusilla, which sets Porter's scenes against another heavyweight actor. Together, Close and Porter give the Capitol side of the story a relationship for viewers to follow, beyond costumes and ceremony.

The role asks for glamour and grief at once. Magno's job is to create spectacle for the Capitol to put on display, and his broken marriage gives him a private wound. Producer Nina Jacobson told TheWrap that Porter is "one of those rare performers who can dazzle and devastate in equal measure on stage and screen."

The thing to watch is whether Porter plays Magno as a man with a wound or as a celebrity in a costume.

Wiress, a victor from District 3, mentors the District 12 team in Sunrise on the Reaping, according to Rotten Tomatoes. That puts her beside Haymitch from the start. Film audiences met her much later in her life, and this story shows where she stood years before.

The casting gives a part that filmgoers remember to an actress whom many younger viewers know first from television. Maya Hawke of Stranger Things takes over a character that Amanda Plummer played in Catching Fire, according to Collider. Many viewers will recognize Hawke before they think of Plummer. The question isn't whether she resembles her predecessor but whether audiences accept her as the same woman at an earlier age. Fans remember Wiress mostly for a repeated phrase, "tick tock," and Hawke has to make that habit believable as something her younger character could grow into. Hawke’s casting pays off if viewers see the Wiress they remember in the younger woman on screen.

Fans of the Hunger Games films know how Mags died far better than how she lived. In Sunrise on the Reaping, Lili Taylor plays Mags years before that ending, as a former champion of the Games, according to Rotten Tomatoes. Parade reports that Lynn Cohen played Mags in Catching Fire, so moviegoers have met this victor only late in her life. Taylor is filling in the earlier years of a woman audiences remember for a single act.

Mags earned her place in moviegoers' memory without saying a word. She never spoke in Catching Fire, according to Parade, and her defining moment on screen came when she sacrificed herself. That leaves Taylor almost nothing on screen to contradict and nearly everything to invent, including Mags's voice, her temperament and the person who made that choice. This is where the casting carries its risk. A younger Mags who talks and acts in a big way could deepen the woman fans grieved, or she could quietly turn her into someone else.

Taylor’s Mags appears only briefly in the trailer, in a hug with Haymitch, Parade reports. In the books, she serves as a mentor for District 12 even though she comes from District 4. If the film keeps that role, looking after another district's tributes gives her a reason to stay at Haymitch's side. It would also point ahead to the sacrifice that later made her matter to fans, when she put others before herself.

Taylor's Mags will be judged on how much she speaks, and on whether her new voice explains the silent woman fans remember or replaces her.

Beetee comes into Sunrise on the Reaping as a past victor, according to Rotten Tomatoes. That gives him standing before the film’s Games even begin, but it doesn’t leave him on the sidelines. He lends his technical expertise to efforts to sabotage the Games, which puts him inside the story’s push against them. The part carries real weight in the plot, and that makes the choice of actor more important than a supporting credit suggests.

Jeffrey Wright played Beetee from Catching Fire onward, according to Variety. The prequel gives the role to Kelvin Harrison Jr., who plays a younger version. Harrison’s task is to create the earlier man that Wright’s version grew out of, without imitating the later performance.

This Beetee is a father as well as a victor. Variety reports that his son, Ampert Latier, is a tribute in the 50th Hunger Games. That is the contest the film follows, so Beetee works on the victors' side while his own child competes in the arena. That father-and-son thread adds personal stakes to a role that already carries weight in the plot.

Harrison's casting will be judged on whether he can play a technician working against the Games while his son is one of their tributes.

Effie Trinket returns as a younger version of an established character, according to The Associated Press. The filmmakers can't build her from nothing, because audiences already know the woman she will become. Elle Fanning plays Effie, Rotten Tomatoes reports, and in this story she works as Haymitch's stylist. As his stylist, she is responsible for how Haymitch looks when he appears before the Capitol, which ties her to the lead from the start.

Fanning will be measured against Elizabeth Banks, who played Effie in the original films. A brand-new character would be judged on her own terms. This Effie is meant to grow into the woman Banks played, so viewers will hold Fanning to that earlier performance whether she wants them to or not. She has to meet two demands at once. Her Effie has to read as the same person audiences remember. She also has to feel like a woman with her own life rather than an impression of Banks. If Fanning copies too closely, she invites the comparison. If she strays too far, fans may not recognize the character at all.

Fanning's success depends less on how much she does on screen than on how quickly viewers stop comparing and accept her as Effie.

Kieran Culkin is taking over a character people already remember, not introducing a new one. Culkin plays the host Caesar Flickerman in Sunrise on the Reaping, according to Rotten Tomatoes. Variety reports that Stanley Tucci played him in all four original films, and that performance is the one Culkin will be measured against. Viewers will also bring a second memory into the theater, since many of them know Culkin as Roman Roy on Succession. Lionsgate Motion Picture Group co-president Erin Westerman says Tucci left fans a Caesar they won't forget, and she expects Culkin to create a version of the host that belongs to him alone. The studio is openly asking for reinvention rather than imitation. The test is whether audiences can stop seeing both Tucci and Roman Roy when Culkin is on screen.

Caesar can look like the franchise's comic relief, but his job on screen is to sell the Games to the Capitol. That job makes him one of the story's sharpest views of the Capitol's cruelty. "A host like Caesar transforms brutality into entertainment, and an actor as layered as Kieran makes sure we don’t look away," Nina Jacobson, a producer at Color Force, said, as reported by Variety. That puts a double demand on Culkin. He has to be charming enough that moviegoers enjoy watching him the way the Capitol crowd does, and unsettling enough that they notice what they are enjoying.

Culkin's Caesar succeeds if he makes viewers uncomfortable with their own attention. If he plays the part only for laughs, the film loses its satire.

The Plutarch Heavensbee who returns in Sunrise on the Reaping has no power yet, and he is far from the man who ran the Games in the later films. Jesse Plemons plays a young version of the character, according to Rotten Tomatoes, rather than the older Plutarch of the original films. CinemaBlend reports that Philip Seymour Hoffman played that older Plutarch. At this stage, Plutarch records the spectacle instead of designing it, working as a cameraman on the crew that films District 12's reaping. Plemons has to cover the distance between that job and the man who later serves as Head Gamemaker of the 75th Hunger Games and then becomes a leader of the rebellion. He has to play a minor figure whose power lies years ahead and still let audiences see the schemer he will become.

This recast carries more weight than most because Plutarch was Hoffman's final film role, according to CinemaBlend, and for many viewers it is the last character they watched him play. Plemons played the son of Hoffman’s cult leader in The Master in 2012, so the role passes to an actor who once played his on-screen son. "His Plutarch will be both a tribute to the character fans have already come to know and a portrayal he makes his own," Erin Westerman, co-president of Lionsgate Motion Picture Group, said, as reported by CinemaBlend. Meeting both aims is hard in a role so closely tied to one actor, and viewers will hold Plemons to that standard.

The bet pays off only if audiences can see, behind a camera on reaping day, the man who will later help lead a rebellion against the Capitol.

#5427. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t said what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#5426. Don’t just use AI to cut costs. Use it to create growth

Bill Gross founded Idealab and has helped create more than 175 companies. He founded and leads Idealab.ai, which publishes the idea framework and the free database referenced in this article, and he is the CEO of ProRata.ai. Idealab.ai is a partner of the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum.

Every CEO I talk to has an AI savings plan. Almost none have an AI revenue plan.

Savings matter. But an AI strategy that stops there is incomplete.

Across 50 years of entrepreneurship, I’ve helped create more than 175 companies. I’ve watched successive technology waves play out the same way. The first instinct is to use the new tool to do the old things cheaper. The companies that win use it to do new things. Electricity didn’t just lower factory power bills; it let factories be rebuilt around the assembly line. The internet didn’t just cut the cost of mailing catalogs; it created Amazon.

An EY-Parthenon survey published in April 2026 found that 63% of growth leaders at large U.S. companies said their organizations were using AI primarily for efficiency and productivity. Just 7% cited diversifying revenue streams. McKinsey’s 2026 research finds that AI high performers pursue growth or innovation alongside efficiency.

In a 2025 study of software and reasoning tasks, METR found that the length of tasks AI agents could complete with 50% reliability had been doubling roughly every seven months. Those lengths reflect how long the tasks take human experts.

AI is making ideas more abundant and early experimentation less expensive. For software-based concepts, it can help teams research a market, write and test code, and build an initial prototype before committing a larger team and budget. The hard part remains choosing the right opportunities, validating demand, and turning them into viable businesses. Established companies can draw on existing expertise and capabilities to get started.

Every established company has expertise in how its industry actually works. Customer knowledge: what people complain about, ask for, pay extra for, and work around. Capabilities built for one purpose that could serve another. Some also have patents, trade secrets, or research shelved because building on them was too expensive to staff. Startups would kill for these. AI can help you explore new uses.

Turning those assets into revenue takes a method. At Idealab, we’ve spent three decades refining 31 ways to find business ideas, grouped into seven lenses. We’ve applied those methods with AI to create a database of more than 1.2 million potential business ideas, freely available at Idealab.ai.

Start from a pain. Fix your own, fix someone else’s, or remove friction, waiting, waste, or danger. Your customer-support logs can reveal problems worth solving.

Make it radically better. Ask what could become dramatically faster, simpler, more convenient, or automated.

Open it to more people. Cut the cost of a premium service so a new customer group can afford it. What would that make possible?

Read the signals people leave. Look for repeated questions and complaints, workarounds, misuse, broken trust, and ignored niches.

Three lenses start from supply, meaning what just became possible:

Harness a new capability. Apply new technology to an old problem, or pair an existing capability with a different business model.

Get the timing right. Look for a falling cost curve, a platform shift, or a regulatory change. Exhume the graveyard: revisit projects shelved because they were right but too early.

Think big. Reimagine a giant but static industry, or start from a bold vision of a better future.

Consider a logistics company that can predict delivery disruptions. Could that expertise support a planning service for smaller shippers? AI can help explore the possibility. Customers still need to demonstrate that the problem matters enough to pay for a solution.

Run these lenses against your expertise, customer knowledge, capabilities, and intellectual property. Use AI to identify and challenge the assumptions, then test demand directly with customers. Assign an accountable owner to the strongest opportunity. Use customer interviews, prototypes, or paid pilots to learn what people actually need and whether they will pay. Give the team clear milestones for deciding whether to invest further, change direction, or stop.

One more thing. Put a revenue target next to the savings target in your next board deck. The goal is to build a stronger company by improving efficiency and creating new sources of growth.

#5425. Apple's camera and photo software chief has retired with no named replacement

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Jon McCormack's former deputies are taking over his duties under other Apple executives, according to Bloomberg

Jon McCormack, Apple $AAPL's head of camera and photo software, left the company through retirement at the end of October, ending a tenure of more than eight years, according to Bloomberg.

Apple has not appointed anyone at the vice president level to fill the position McCormack held, according to Bloomberg. His onetime deputies now handle the work he led, each reporting to other executives. An Apple spokesperson declined to comment.

McCormack was responsible for the Camera and Photos apps, along with the core technology behind how users shoot, browse and edit photos and video, according to Bloomberg. He reported to Craig Federighi, Apple's senior vice president of software engineering. The retirement puts Federighi in charge of managing a handover of leadership in a niche, technical field.

Among the projects McCormack led was the iPhone 17 lineup's redesigned selfie camera, which debuted last year, according to Bloomberg. Apple also built a variable-aperture camera into the iPhone 18 Pro lineup this year, and it rolled out a customizable Camera app interface with professional controls.

McCormack objected to generative AI being used to make or change photos, because he thought an image ought to depict something that really happened, according to Bloomberg. That view clashes with the direction Apple has lately taken by adopting AI-powered tools. His retirement did not stem from any dispute with Apple about its AI strategy.

Google $GOOGL, a unit of Alphabet, and Samsung Electronics have rolled out generative AI tools that let users substantially alter their pictures, according to Bloomberg.

In a June interview with Tyler Stalman, McCormack discussed iOS 27 features including Clean Up, Extend and Spatial Reframing. He said the features "preserve the integrity of the moment," according to 9to5Mac.

McCormack is another vice president to exit Apple this fall, following Jennifer Bailey, who led Apple Pay and Wallet services for many years, according to Bloomberg. Chief Executive Officer John Ternus has shaken up management, aiming to help Apple operate with more speed and efficiency.

#5424. Verizon’s CEO knows Elon Musk is coming for his business. He says it’ll cost SpaceX over $300 billion to compete

Elon Musk wants Starlink to become a major U.S. phone carrier. Verizon CEO Dan Schulman says that if Musk pulls it off, he’ll have spent four to six years and about $300 billion building a copy of Verizon.

“At the end of the day, he might have a network that is pretty much exactly like our network today,” Schulman told Fortune Editor in Chief Alyson Shontell on the latest episode of Fortune’s Titans and Disruptors of Industry podcast. “There’s no secret sauce, there’s no magic wand, there’s no structural cost advantage that will come out. He’ll have a network, and in four years, five, six years, he’ll be the sixth entrant into the market.”

Musk added to that picture Wednesday, telling the New York Times DealBook Summit that SpaceX is looking into the production of “micro cell towers” for Starlink Mobile as early as next year, referring to ground hardware that Schulman says turns SpaceX into just another carrier.

Last month, Elon Musk’s SpaceX announced plans for satellite internet service Starlink to become “a major mobile carrier in the U.S.,” sending telecom stocks plunging and market caps for the three major U.S. carriers sliding by $50 billion. Verizon alone dropped 8.7%, marking its worst single-day performance since 2002.

SpaceX acquired wireless spectrum from telecommunications company Echostar in a $17 billion deal in September 2025, which, following Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approval in May, laid the groundwork for the company to launch the Starlink Mobile, which would differ from other carriers by not requiring a dish or router, but by connecting photos directly to satellites.

The company’s October announcement included an update the FCC has approved 15,000 new satellite launches under Starlink Mobile, as well as SpaceX’s acquisition of an additional 14 MHz of paired 800 MHz low-band spectrum licenses from Grain Management.

Schulman already sees the market as competitive, with two major cable companies and three mobile network operators occupying it and anticipates the industry looking and feeling “radically different” three or four years into the future. An incoming 6G world will pave the way for high-speed broadband nationally, as well as an AI fabric across Verizon’s network that will usher in additional uses for agentic technologies. The need to continue moving forward exists whether or not SpaceX becomes a main player.

“I think the right thing to do is to believe everything that SpaceX says they’re going to do, that they do, and they do it with excellence,” Schulman said. “There’s no downside to thinking that and preparing for that. The downside is when you’re complacent about it.”

In a note to investors last month, JPMorgan Chase analysts said without a deal with an existing wireless carrier, SpaceX would need to construct its own terrestrial network to go toe-to-toe with competitors, an immense undertaking that would require even more capital than what the satellite company is already spending on spectrum that enables wireless communications in the first place.

“We continue to see limited near-term risk to U.S. wireless incumbents given the time, infrastructure and capital required to build a competitive terrestrial network,” analysts said.

The Verizon CEO said he hasn’t recently spoken with Musk, but said Musk has a series of next moves he can make, either SpaceX invests further in data centers in space or pursue a “whole host of high ROI potential returns. Schulman added that Musk’s strategy remains unclear to him.

“What is clear is any scenario or any possibility, we are thinking about it and getting prepared for any of it, and that is, you know, what I tell the company: let’s be ready,” he said. “No matter what the scenario is, be prepared and shape the market, not react.”

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5423. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

#5422. Anthropic stock pops 30% to $2 trillion market cap in mega IPO

Anthropic’s stock surged more than 30% in first minutes as a public company, a roaring debut that crowned the AI company—at least briefly—with a stunning, $2 trillion market cap.

Shares of Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share on Thursday, up 34% from the $83 IPO price. The stock pop began to moderate somewhat as the trading day continued, with shares trading up 14%, at $94.50 per share.

Shares of Anthropic, under the ticker symbol “ANT,” began trading a couple of hours after the stock market’s opening bell. The strong demand for Anthropic shares came as the broader market was under pressure, with the Nasdaq down 363 points and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 1038 points in midday trading.

At the $111.50 opening price, Anthropic’s market cap was roughly $2 trillion—an astounding Wall Street debut that instantly puts the five-year-old AI company in the elite club of trillion-dollar public companies.

“This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a statement posted on X on Thursday.

Anthropic priced the offering Wednesday night at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, giving the company a $1.5 trillion valuation. Demand was strong enough that it raised the deal to 980 million shares from 825 million.

There had been endless speculation about whether Anthropic would top SpaceX as the largest IPO of all time. At a $1.5 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion ($81.4 billion, if stock sold by insiders is included) topped the $75 billion raised by SpaceX.

Seven strategic partners, including Google and Nvidia, have also agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Anthropic stock at the IPO price. And the deal’s underwriters also have a “greenshoe” option to purchase an additional 147 million shares of Anthropic stock. If exercised, that would bring the total proceeds of Anthropic’s IPO to $118 billion.

The offering will provide Anthropic with a vital infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. It will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic. At least 400 early hires will be worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC.

“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said in his statement Thursday. “We will not bend to either business or political pressure,” Amodei said, invoking the company’s stated commitment to develop AI technology with safeguards.

Anticipation for the IPOs of Anthropic and its arch-rival OpenAI has been building ever since OpenAI ignited the generative AI boom in late 2022 with the launch of ChatGPT. With OpenAI holding off on its IPO until at least 2027, Anthropic becomes the first pure-play maker of frontier AI models to go public (SpaceX also does rockets, and Google and Meta both have massive businesses in search and social media).

But the Anthropic IPO also comes at a tenuous time for the AI industry. It’s been barely a week since the AI industry lost one of its most powerful figures. Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last Thursday, following reports that he had engaged in two extramarital affairs: one with a customer suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese intelligence asset, and one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. His exit added fresh pressure to a listing that was already seen as a stress test of investors’ appetite for AI.

Analysts and investors told Fortune they didn’t expect the Nvidia shock to derail the offering or touch Anthropic’s core business. The bigger risk, they said, may come later. Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg warned that turmoil at Nvidia could bring Anthropic “much tougher questions” once it starts reporting quarterly results as a public company. Georgetown’s Jason Schloetzer predicted closer scrutiny of Anthropic’s ties to Nvidia and to customers associated with the chipmaker.

Anthropic’s revenue has soared thanks to strong demand from business customers, a market in which Anthropic has been especially successfull. In the nine months ending September 30, Anthropic generated $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. The company posted a $104 billion net loss in its most recent nine-month period, though the bulk of the red ink is because of the way it accounted for its convertible notes.

But the high share price straight out of the gates will put immense pressure on Anthropic as it seeks to justify its valuation to investors and to prove that AI tools can deliver the massive payoff Wall Street expects.

Anthropic CEO Amodei, once the VP of research at OpenAI, left to cofound Anthropic at the end of 2020, along with sister Daniella and several other OpenAI employees, when they became disillusioned with OpenAI’s approach to AI safety. Still, the company’s IPO prospectus is replete with warnings of the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence including “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The IPO also comes amid growing public backlash to AI data centers, underscored by the results of the U.S. midterm elections. High profile incidents of rogue AI agents, by OpenAI as well as Anthropic, have added to the unease over the technology.

The stakes reach well beyond one company. Anthropic has more than 400 backers, and nearly every major venture firm owns a piece of it, so the IPO is effectively a liquidity event for the AI boom itself. A strong debut and a stable stretch of trading afterward would suggest the boom has more runway. A stumble would be read as a sign the bubble is near its peak. At least one investor argued that Huang’s departure could even help Anthropic: CEO Dario Amodei had clashed with Huang over chip exports to China and over AI regulation.

Several Wall Street research firms, including Wolfe Research, Citizens, and Melius Research initiated coverage of Anthropic with buy ratings.

#5421. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”

Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate issue,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.
