#5420. Kalshi and Polymarket claim 98% accuracy in calling midterm races

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A New York Times analysis found prediction markets did no better than election forecasts for most of the race

Kalshi said the candidates its traders favored won 98% of resolved races in Tuesday's midterm elections. The company announced the figure on Wednesday.

The tally covers 479 of 487 races resolved as of 6 a.m. ET on Nov. 4, Kalshi said. Favorites won 356 of 360 House races, 32 of 33 Senate races and 33 of 34 governor races.

Polymarket said that, judged against the day before the election, 98.4% of its settled contests had pointed to the correct winner, according to The Hill. Polymarket put its hit rate at roughly 97% for the Senate and gubernatorial contests and at 98.6% for those in the House.

Kalshi said its markets for House control passed 99% likelihood at 8:10 p.m. ET and its Senate control markets passed 99% at 9 p.m. ET, hours ahead of the networks. Trading volume on its 2026 midterm markets topped $2.5 billion, compared with $1.3 billion for the 2024 cycle, the company said.

In a separate analysis, Kalshi said directional accuracy for races called by 6:26 a.m. ET on Nov. 4 rose from 93.8% three months out to 98.2% when polls closed. Brier scores, on which lower is better, fell from 0.040 to 0.016, the company said.

Outside experts urged caution. Ross Dahlke, a University of Wisconsin-Madison professor, said the figures include only resolved markets, which may be easier to predict, and that many races were fairly certain going into Election Day, according to The Hill.

An analysis by The New York Times found that prediction markets fared about the same as election forecasts through most of the midterm campaign. Markets gained an edge in the closing days, the Times said, once polls and forecasts had gone out of date. Kalshi told the Times that its ability to post odds on par with seasoned forecasters well ahead of voting demonstrated the markets’ forecasting strength.

Polymarket did not respond to a request for comment from The New York Times.

Koleman Strumpf, an economics professor at Wake Forest University who studies prediction markets, gave the markets a B, according to Bloomberg. He said the markets pointed the right way but underestimated how large the Democratic wave would be.

Kalshi said on X $TWTR that its markets outperformed forecasting models including those of Silver Bulletin, FiftyPlusOne and The Economist, according to Bloomberg. Nate Silver, who runs Silver Bulletin, said his model and others showed the Democratic wave sooner and more aggressively.

#5419. iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year

The fashion business thrives on the conceit that it is modern, on-trend, and all about what’s happening right now. But behind the scenes—in the textile mills and garment factories that supply major brands—is an industry that runs much as it did in the 1970s. Its supply chains are splintered, chaotic, and based in warehouses that are so old-fashioned they may not even be on the internet, according to Max Easton, CEO of Smartex.AI.Most of the work is done by hand. Checking the quality of the fabric, for instance, will be performed by a worker holding a handful of color swatches, watching a roll of cloth go by all day.“They’re looking for simple physical defects like holes, needles, the wrong yarn, something that would be noticeable in a garment, right?” Easton said to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon this year. For most brands, there is no such thing as a “white” T-shirt. It needs to be exactly the right shade of white—which might be a brilliant white or a creamier off-white.

But because the work is inspected by humans, fashion brands can never be quite sure that the quality of the fabric they’re buying is going to be consistent, or even match what they ordered.

“If you go to any kind of [fashion] supply chain, whether it’s fabric production or garment production, most people are just kind of amazed by how chaotic it is,” Easton said.

The company has been working with Tony Fadell, the legendary codesigner of the iPod, iPhone, and Nest doorbell, to launch a physical AI product that can perform fabric quality checks continuously, at three times the speed of a human. Fadell—who has invested roughly $10 million in the company—is coming aboard as Smartex’s chairman. H&M, also an investor in Smartex, is one of its launch customers. Smartex has about 65 employees, revenues in the low millions annually, and has installed 800 of its older monitoring systems at clients in 10 different countries. The company’s valuation four years ago was $55 million; Easton declined to give an updated number.

The company is rolling out two new products: Smartex Inspect is a physical AI camera system that attaches to existing textile machinery to monitor the quality of the material as it goes by. And Smartex IQ generates intelligence from the supply-chain data that comes from Smartex’s suite of products.

Fabric inspection is “very, very technical, and it’s highly prone to human error,” Fadell told Fortune. “Depending on whether it’s in the morning or in the afternoon or on Friday afternoon … it’s all subjective. There’s no Pantone color for quality inspection.

“If you walked into a mill or a garment facility 50 years ago, and you walk into it today, it’s almost exactly the same—same processes, same equipment, same everything. It’s not been upgraded in any way. They might have email. In some cases they don’t even have Wi-Fi,” he said.

Companies are at the mercy of independent operators in multiple foreign countries. “They have zero visibility, even when [the product] arrives. They don’t know when it’s going to arrive,” Easton said.

For any player in the apparel chain, 50% of their cost base is fabric. But because the product is so variable in quality, a company like H&M will typically over-order about 5% more fabric than they need—in the sure knowledge that some of it won’t be good enough to use.

“So globally [at H&M], that’s like 2.5 billion meters of fabric every single year, just in case,” Easton says. At $4 a meter, that adds up to $10 billion in fabric costs. Easton reckons Smartex might save H&M $100 million annually simply by reducing its waste.

There are four things that H&M cares about, Fadell said: price, speed, quality, and sustainability. “A lot of times they commit to making this garment. They presell it online, but they can’t deliver it because the fabric shows up at the garment house, and they can’t make the garment because the fabric’s wrong in some way,” he said. “Reducing waste means better margins.”

The challenge isn’t as simple as pointing a camera at a textile processor and sending it to a computer. The system has to take into account changes in lighting, the speed at which the fabric is moving, small variations in color, and calibrate all that against a client’s own standards. Smartex has a library of 50 billion images of fabric to do that.

It is, admittedly, somewhat odd to hear Fadell—famed for creating some of the most iconic consumer products ever made—enthusing over loom quality and stitching. Still, he said: “This is something I’ve been investing in for a decade now, because I believe in very, very applied AI in the physical world, but you’ve got to make it really easy for the customers to use.”

Jim Edwards is the executive editor for global news at Fortune. He was previously the editor-in-chief of Business Insider's news division and the founding editor of Business Insider UK. His investigative journalism has changed the law in two U.S. federal districts and two states. The U.S. Supreme Court cited his work on the death penalty in the concurrence to Baze v. Rees, the ruling on whether lethal injection is cruel or unusual. He also won the Neal award for an investigation of bribes and kickbacks on Madison Avenue.

#5418. I tested an AI startup that claimed it could beat Wall Street earnings estimates. It won 40 out of 50 times

In 1997, a Fortune journalist observed, “The simplest, most visible, most merciless measure of corporate success … has become this one: Did you make your earnings last quarter?” Those words hold up just as well today. Indeed, the current Q3 earnings season has featured the same, decades-old ritual: Investors wait to discover if a firm can meet or exceed a consensus target from Wall Street analysts—and then reward or punish the company’s share price accordingly. Now, that ritual could be in for a shake-up.

In October, I was approached by a financial AI startup called Samaya that claimed it could predict earnings outcomes more accurately than the analysts. Prove it, I said. I invited Samaya, which raised $43 million from prominent investors in 2025, to put its money where its mouth is and provide Q3 predictions for 50 big companies, ranging from Coca-Cola to Carvana, prior to their earnings releases.

The company accepted the challenge. This led to a two-week experiment in which we placed Samaya’s AI predictions alongside the consensus view of Wall Street analysts in a spreadsheet, and then recorded the actual Q3 earnings number. Samaya didn’t just beat the analysts, it smoked them. For 40 out of the 50 companies, the AI startup’s forecasts were more accurate than the Wall Street consensus and, in most of these cases, by a considerable margin.

The experiment represents a small sample over a single earnings period, but it has potentially large implications for investors, companies, and analysts alike. More broadly, the exercise underscored, once again, how AI is transforming many aspects of corporate America.

For anyone unfamiliar with earnings season, it goes like this: The season kicks off a few weeks after the close of a calendar quarter, and enters full swing when a cluster of big banks report their results, followed by a range of other sectors. Prior to each company’s earnings release, a handful of companies, including FactSet and Zacks, publish a consensus estimate that reflects the average of analyst predictions for a given company’s performance. When the actual earnings results go live, any meaningful divergence from “the Street’s” prediction leads investors to drive the price of the stock up in the event of a beat, and way down if there is a miss.

For purposes of the AI versus analysts experiment, Fortune and Samaya selected 50 companies that reported Q3 earnings between Oct. 26 and Nov. 5, covering 10 different sectors ranging from health care to energy to IT. In each case, Samaya supplied an AI-based estimate for the most important metric (EPS [earnings per share] or revenue) for a given company at least a day before its earnings release. For comparison, the exercise used an analyst consensus view supplied by Bloomberg.

When the first results rolled in, it became clear Samaya was not blowing smoke. The startup had forecast that Verizon would bring in $34.52 billion in revenue—a number closer to the actual figure of $34.31 billion than $34.77 billion, which was the consensus figure from the analysts. Likewise with UPS, where Samaya’s prediction for adjusted EPS of $1.65 was more accurate than the $1.62 consensus estimate. (The actual figure was $1.67.)

After losing to AI on the first four companies to report, the analysts struck back, producing more accurate estimates for the next two, S&P Global and PayPal. But from then on, it was a rout; Samaya supplied better picks for 36 of the remaining 44 companies. Its notable wins included Palantir (where it predicted $2.30 billion in revenue versus the actual figure of $2.31 billion and $2.18 billion for the analysts) and energy giant Permian Resources, where Samaya forecast the actual EPS figure of $0.69 exactly, while the Street had predicted $0.625.

Samaya’s most notable miss came with Yum Brands. The AI startup’s EPS forecast of $1.42 fell well short of the food giant’s actual EPS of $1.56, while the analysts came closer with a forecast of $1.49. Samaya also lost to the analysts when it came to forecasting the degree to which tech giants Amazon and Google would fall short of revenue expectations.

Samaya CEO Maithra Raghu points out that, where the Street consensus proved more accurate, it was typically in the case of very big companies that are the subject of large volumes of private research. Most of this research did not form part of Samaya’s training material, she said, explaining that the startup relied instead on publicly available data like filings, news reports, and interview transcripts.

Raghu says that Samaya, whose clients include banks and hedge funds, is likely to add analyst notes to training data for earnings in the future. But she also expressed a concern that doing so could bias the AI by teaching it to internalize the same sort of desire for consensus that defines many Wall Street analysts.

“I think there is safety in numbers,” said Sheraz Mian, director of research at Zacks, one of the firms that compiles analyst consensus figures. Mian is an analyst himself, so he is more than familiar with how a Wall Street consensus emerges—a process that is rooted equally in human nature and what is often a tacit pressure game by companies.

According to Mian, there are times when an analyst may believe that a company’s quarterly earnings will fall well outside what most people expect. But he says that there are incentives not to go out on a limb and say so. Namely, the potential acclaim that comes with correctly publishing an unorthodox forecast is unlikely to outweigh the reputational damage an analyst will incur if such a forecast is wrong. On balance, there is an unspoken incentive to stick with the herd.

This instinct to conform is reinforced by corporate investor relations teams, which are facing powerful incentives of their own when it comes to earnings targets. In an observation that is as true today as when it was written, the Fortune story from 1997 noted: “The price of missing a quarter has risen sharply, particularly among high-priced growth stocks. In the growth stock fraternity, ‘missing by a penny’ now implies the height of corporate boneheadedness.”

And indeed, the history of earnings in recent decades shows that, while exceeding forecasts typically offers stocks a modest boost, missing those forecasts—even by a little—results in investors punishing the stock by a disproportionate measure. One result of this phenomenon, Mian explains, is that investor relations (IR) teams monitor individual analysts closely, and are quick to call them up, especially if they believe a forecast is too optimistic.

Even though a rule change by the Securities and Exchange Commission in 2000, known as Regulation Fair Disclosure, forbids companies from providing material information—including their forthcoming earnings—to analysts, they are still able to exert considerable soft pressure, says Mian.

“In the long run, they provide optimistic numbers that get walked down to beatable targets at the end, so a higher proportion of companies end up meeting or beating expectations right at the close,” says Paul Hribar, a professor of accounting at the University of Iowa.

Hribar also observes that, in response to all this, there has long been the idea of a “whisper number” on Wall Street—a figure that is closer to what people actually believe than what is stated in public predictions. But if AI models like Samaya’s gain traction, it’s an open question as to whether the current earnings ritual of coming up with a “consensus” number, or even a whisper version of it, will persist.

After all, the current earnings regime is highly rooted in human incentives and bias—qualities that are not shared by insentient AI models. It’s possible, of course, that the AI models will in time internalize these biases as well, and reflect them in their output—a possibility that Raghu, Samaya’s CEO, explicitly noted. But it’s equally possible that the growth of AI-based forecasts could blow up the cozy analyst-IR consensus altogether.

The apparent success of Samaya’s model also raises the question of whether Raghu, a former member of the foundational Google Brain AI team, might decide to ditch startup life in favor of trading stocks. She says the question is “not uncommon” but that her plans for now are instead to keep working on Samaya’s technology.

Jeff John Roberts is the Finance and Crypto editor at Fortune, overseeing coverage of the blockchain and how technology is changing finance.

#5417. Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

“No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”

#5416. 12 numbers that define Denny Hamlin’s NASCAR career as he weighs retiring

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Denny Hamlin has 64 Cup wins and no championship. 12 numbers show why he is torn about retiring after 2027.

A career built on this much winning usually ends with a championship, and a championship is the one thing missing from Hamlin's. For all those victories, he has won zero Cup Series titles, according to NASCAR.com. He has come close enough for the zero to hurt, finishing second in the standings in 2010 and again in 2025. Kyle Larson won the 2025 title at Phoenix, according to The Associated Press. One near miss came early in Hamlin's career and the other came late in it, so the missing title is a pattern rather than one unlucky year.

NASCAR's format rewards the driver who is sharpest when the title is decided, and one driver of Hamlin's era has managed that again and again. Larson has won three Cup titles, according to . His record shows that a driver of Hamlin's generation can win the championship more than once under this format. The question about Hamlin, then, is not whether he is good enough. It is whether he can put his best stretch of the season into the 10 races that decide the title.

A driver weighing retirement has usually stopped winning, and Hamlin's 2026 shows the opposite. He won four races, NASCAR.com reports, with an early victory at Las Vegas and then three straight wins in a summer run at Nashville, Tenn., Michigan and Pocono. Winning more than once a year is routine for him, and 2026 extended his streak of multi-win seasons to eight. That makes this season part of a pattern that has run for most of a decade. The real question is when he won those races.

Hamlin still had the speed to win in 2026. Of the four races in which he ran the fastest laps, he won three, according to MotorBiscuit. On the days he was quickest on the track, he usually finished first. For a driver deciding whether to step away, that kind of pace is a sign that he hasn't slowed down.

Most drivers have a track that suits them, and Hamlin's is Pocono Raceway, where his eight Cup wins are the most any driver has earned at the track, according to NASCAR.com. That record is more than a personal statistic, because it is the standard every other Cup driver at Pocono is chasing. For a driver who has never won a championship, the Pocono mark is one record that belongs to him alone.

Pocono is where Hamlin's winning began, and it is still where he wins, which matters to a driver deciding when to stop. He won his first Cup race there in 2006. He earned his eighth win at the track in June 2026, according to Motorsport.com, in the season he is now weighing as a possible farewell. If age were wearing down his driving, a decline would likely show at his best track, and his latest result there shows none. That gives the case for staying one of its strongest arguments: he is still winning where he has always won.

Denny Hamlin will have raced 22 Cup Series seasons if he drives through the end of his current contract in 2027, according to NASCAR.com. Heavy reports that he has driven for Joe Gibbs Racing throughout his Cup career. The 22 is a measure of loyalty as much as longevity, because every one of those seasons would belong to the same team.

Hamlin left himself room even after he signed. He agreed to the extension in July 2025, and when he was asked about it after the announcement, he said it would probably be his last contract, according to Heavy. That makes 22 seasons the earliest plausible stopping point, not a farewell he has scheduled. A driver who hedges about his final deal is saving the decision for later, so the last year of the contract settles nothing by itself.

The strongest push for a longer career is coming from Hamlin's team rather than from Hamlin himself. Owner Joe Gibbs has begun pressing Hamlin to keep racing, NASCAR.com reports, and the team hopes to have him behind the wheel in 2028. That season comes after his current deal ends, so the team is asking for more than he has agreed to give. Another season is a standing offer, not a hypothetical. The pressure from his owner shows that Joe Gibbs Racing still sees him as a driver worth keeping in the car.

Hamlin measures his remaining time in chances to win, while his team measures it in seasons, and the two do not produce the same answer. He also describes what lies ahead in narrow terms. "But we've only got one more shot at this," Hamlin said. He sees his future as a single chance, while his team is already planning for 2028. The case for staying depends on whether a title is still within reach, not on how long he can keep racing.

Hamlin is asking his team to share responsibility for his final push for a title. He wants Joe Gibbs Racing to improve his No. 11 team for 2027, according to NASCAR.com, and that makes whatever the organization does this offseason part of how his career ends. He did not present the request as a complaint. He paired it with a promise to raise his own game. "And it's no secret — I definitely want Joe Gibbs Racing to look in the mirror as well and figure out how they can make my (No.) 11 team better next year and what we need to do to be better, because I'm certainly going to do that as a driver," Hamlin said. By tying his effort to the team's in public, he has asked owner Joe Gibbs's organization to match him. The question for 2027 is less whether Hamlin still has the skill and more whether the people around him will give him a car worthy of his last contracted season.

Credit: Zach Catanzareti Photo / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

NASCAR fans tend to assume the Cup Series champion is the driver who was best all season. Under the sport's playoff format, the title goes to the driver who runs best in the final stretch of races, and that is not always the same person. In 2026 it wasn't. Denny Hamlin posted the best average finish of any Cup driver that year, according to FOX Sports, but Kyle Larson won the championship. Larson made no claim to the stronger season. "This was statistically probably one of our worst years," Larson told The Associated Press. Under these rules, a driver can win races for two decades and never become champion, and that is what has happened to Hamlin.

Hamlin is still winning, still without a title and now close to the end of his career. Age has not yet shown up in his results, and 2026 was the most consistent season of his career. His time to add a title is short, though, because his current contract runs through the 2027 Cup season, according to Heavy. Hamlin has acknowledged that a driver cannot take back a retirement once he announces it, so he has to decide while he is still winning.

NASCAR.com summed up Hamlin's career through its key figures as he considered whether to retire. Those figures cover his record at Pocono Raceway, the Daytona 500 he has won more than once, the championship he has never won, and his own words about aging and when to step away. Some of the numbers argue for staying and others argue for leaving, and the slides that follow weigh which side each one supports. The question behind every slide is whether one more season can bring Hamlin the title that two decades of winning have not.

Denny Hamlin has 64 Cup wins, ninth in Cup Series history, according to NASCAR.com, and he reached that total while still racing in his mid-40s. Richard Petty holds the record with 200 wins, a total from an earlier era that no current driver can expect to reach. Hamlin already belongs among the sport’s great winners. What he lacks lies elsewhere.

Hamlin is still adding to that total. His count began with his first Cup win in 2006, and after the late races of 2026 he still appeared as an active driver among the sport's all-time winners, according to NASCAR.com. His winning has also held up with age, and he has won more than once in each of the last eight seasons. That record shows steady success year after year rather than a late burst. Whenever he walks away, he will leave while the wins are still coming, not after they have dried up.

For a driver with this record, staying on makes sense only if he can still win. Hamlin rejects the idea of hanging on just to fill a seat. "I'm just too much of a competitor to just go out there and make laps," Hamlin told NASCAR.com. He judges any extra season by whether he can contend, the same standard that produced his career total. The wins prove he can still compete, and the decision turns on what they haven't brought him.

In 2026, the title was settled before Hamlin could do anything about it in the last race. Larson clinched the championship in the finale's opening stage, The Associated Press reports, and Hamlin was not even his closest challenger in points going into that race. Hamlin judged the year as a strong one with a single clear failure. "I guess the lows (are) not winning it all. Other than that, we sustained pretty good performance through the whole year," Hamlin said.

His wins are already in the record book, but the title is not, and the chance to change that zero gives him his strongest reason to race one more season.

Hamlin went into the 2026 playoff as the top seed and still ended the year third in the standings, NASCAR.com reports, with Kyle Larson taking the championship. He wasn’t even the strongest title threat on his own team. Christopher Bell, his Joe Gibbs Racing teammate, entered the finale as Larson’s closest challenger, according to The Associated Press.

Hamlin lost the championship over several weeks, not in one bad night. Larson took the points lead from him after the third playoff race, RACER reports, and Hamlin never got it back. By the last race he trailed by 70 points and needed an outright win, and Larson clinched the title in the finale’s first stage.

Hamlin traces Larson's title to how hard Larson drives. "There is a little bit more variance in the results because of how hard he pushes it, but he reaps the benefits because he gets lots of wins," Hamlin told RACER. By his own account, he lost to a driver who accepts more risk and collects wins because of it. Hamlin didn't treat the result as a wound either. Asked how losing the title felt, he said he felt nothing.

For a driver weighing one more year, the result supports both sides of the decision. He showed in 2026 that he can still earn the top seed, which suggests another title run is possible, but the same season shows how quickly the playoff can take that advantage away.

Hamlin started the title fight as the favorite on paper, after he won the regular season and took the No. 1 seed. He then went without a win across the 10-race Chase, according to MotorBiscuit. Over that many races, a winless stretch means a real dip in form, not one bad afternoon. Hamlin admitted the drop himself. "It did drop a little bit in The Chase; there's no doubt about that if you look at average running position, things like that," Hamlin said.

Four wins prove he can still win races. What 2027 has to show is whether he can do it when the championship is at stake.

Hamlin averaged an 8.9 finish in 2026, the best of his career, according to NASCAR.com, and the best of any full-season driver. Tyler Reddick came closest with a 12.2 average, according to FOX Sports.

Hamlin could only average that low by running near the front almost every weekend, and he did. He placed in the top 10 in 24 races, more than in any season since 2021, so his average came from good results week after week rather than from a handful of standout days. Hamlin felt that consistency from behind the wheel. "This was the most put-together year I think I've ever had," he said. For a driver weighing retirement, this steadiness is the strongest part of the record, because it shows he was complete across the whole year and not only fast now and then.

Hamlin earned those finishes during the races rather than relying on where he started them. His average starting position was 9.8, according to FOX Sports, and on a typical weekend he finished ahead of where he began. A driver gains those spots through strategy, passing and staying out of trouble, and that work depends on him more than on the raw speed of his car.

In 2026, Hamlin raced as a driver at the top of his craft, not one hanging on.

Hamlin didn’t just win at Pocono in 2026. He won comfortably, finishing 1.678 seconds ahead of runner-up Tyler Reddick, according to Motorsport.com.

At Pocono, Hamlin has shown he can still win where he has won before. He has yet to show he can win when a championship depends on the result.

A missing championship hasn't stopped Hamlin from collecting the sport's biggest single-race trophies. NASCAR.com reports that Hamlin took the Daytona 500 in 2016 and again in consecutive years, 2019 and 2020, for three wins in all. His trophies from the sport's other crown-jewel races include three Southern 500s and a Coca-Cola $KO 600. Whatever has kept him from a championship, it isn't an inability to win when a single race carries the most prestige.

Hamlin very nearly lost the first of those Daytona wins. He beat Martin Truex Jr. by 0.010 seconds in 2016, the closest finish in Daytona 500 history, according to CBC. Hamlin gave much of the credit for that win to the drivers around him. "But this wouldn't be possible if it wasn't for Toyotas sticking together all race long," he said. At Daytona, a driver needs other cars to push him through the draft.

As Hamlin weighs one more season, his Daytona record gives him reasons both to stay and to leave. He has the skill and composure to win the sport's biggest single day, and that is a reason to keep chasing major prizes. But winning one race by a margin that small, with help from other drivers, is a different test from winning a title over a full playoff.

Hamlin has shown on three occasions that he can win the Daytona 500. What he has never done is carry that kind of form through a full playoff to a title.

Hamlin will base his exit on his ability to win races, and the number of years behind him plays no part in it. "I want the ability to know I can win my last race," Hamlin told Heavy. His test and the contract's end date are at odds, because as long as he keeps winning, reaching the end of the deal becomes a reason to continue rather than to stop. Joe Gibbs Racing President Dave Alpern judges him by the same standard, and he says Hamlin can win in any given week and that he can't tell yet when age will slow him down. With the driver and the team both measuring him by wins, and neither seeing the end, the count could climb past 22.

The 22nd season is less a scheduled goodbye than the year that shows whether he still passes his own test.

Most drivers retire when their results force them out, but Hamlin has set his own rule. At 46, he will keep racing only as long as he can contend for wins, NASCAR.com reports, and he is weighing an exit now because of the aging he notices in his daily life, not in his finishes.

Hamlin expects age to catch up with him even while he believes he is driving as well as he ever has. "Father Time is undefeated. I can feel it," Hamlin said. He says the changes are already plain to him in everyday life, and he expects them to reach his racing eventually. For him, the open question is when the decline arrives on the track, not whether he is good enough today. Part of his decision, then, rests on his own sense of how age is affecting him, not only on what his results show. Waiting for his results to fall off could mean breaking his own rule, because by then he might already have raced a season without contending.

Any 2027 season is a bet that he can make one more real run at the title before the decline he feels reaches the race track.

Hamlin does not plan to settle the question inside his own garage. He intends to consult Kevin Harvick, a retired driver who has already made the choice Hamlin faces now, so he will weigh the team's push against advice from outside it.

Joe Gibbs Racing can make the offer, but only Hamlin can judge whether one more season is a real shot at a title or just more laps.

Hamlin reached the part of 2026 that decides the championship with less energy than at any other point in the year. He didn’t use fatigue as an excuse, but he didn’t hide it either. “I think I certainly probably burned myself out by the end of the year,” Hamlin said. By his own account, he used up much of the energy he needed to turn the strongest regular season in the field into a title.

The dip in his form was slight, but it came in exactly the weeks when NASCAR awards its championship. The open question is whether he can reach the final stretch of a season with enough left to contend.

For a driver weighing one last season, stamina at the end of the year matters more than speed at the start of it.

Hamlin’s request concerns performance, not pay. He has said he would not race two or three more years unless he could win every weekend, which rules out a long, gradual exit.

A better car won’t decide his future by itself, but without one, there’s no 2028.

#5415. Unless you’re building a data center or have a side hustle, you’re significantly worse off than last year, according to the Fed

Visit a grocery store or gas station, and you’ll notice prices across the U.S. keep climbing. On top of that, the Federal Reserve’s latest minutes suggest that unless you’re in two very niche groups of consumers, you’re probably markedly worse off in terms of income in 2026 compared with last year.By its very nature, inflation erodes spending power as prices rise. But in a balanced economy, when inflation is at its target of 2%, those increases are offset by income growth, so consumers can still afford goods and services without seeking additional income or eating into their savings.But in 2026, inflation has been well above the 2% target. The latest inflation readings from the Bureau of Labor Statistics came in at 3.7% over the past 12 months, through September 2026. However, in addition to prices rising above the central bank’s 2% target, Fed minutes from the latest Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting showed wage growth for most industries lagged well behind price increases.

The affordability conundrum facing households is therefore twofold: Not only are prices rising quicker than consumers can reasonably expect, but any increases to their income are coming in well short of the new demands on their purse strings.

The Fed minutes from the meeting ended Oct. 28 read that most participants “judged that aggregate nominal wage growth remained moderate and was broadly consistent with the committee’s 2% inflation objective.”

Some sectors are posting wage growth, the minutes noted: Many members “observed that shortages of skilled workers needed for data center construction and related industries had contributed to sizable wage premiums in those industries, while a few noted that reduced labor supply in industries reliant on immigrant workers could add to sectoral wage pressures, although these developments did not appear to be having a material effect on aggregate wage measures.”

These factors are potentially good news for the Fed because they suggest the U.S. is not on the cusp of an inflationary wage-price spiral—making it easier for the FOMC to bring inflation back to its mandated 2% target. A wage-price spiral refers to a feedback loop in which higher labor costs push up production and consumer demand, leading workers to demand higher incomes again to offset the increased cost of living.

However, while it’s one less headache for the Fed, incomes lagging inflation by nearly 2% means consumers already stretched are being spread even thinner.

“Fed members acknowledged that wage growth is consistent with their inflation target—but inflation is not consistent with their target,” noted UBS chief economist Paul Donovan to clients this morning. “This is a subtle way of saying that wages are falling behind inflation.”

But in addition to the industries benefiting from the AI infrastructure boom, Donovan points out that the Fed’s notes convey that “consumer resilience continues to depend on lowering savings rates and engaging in side hustles. It implies labor cost pressures are not an inflation driver.”

The Fed has a few weeks and a handful of data releases before its next rate-setting meeting in December. However, the meeting notes state that the economy is “stable and close to maximum employment” while inflation is ahead of target; this suggests tensions in the Fed’s mandate may call for a rate hike.

Interest rate traders assign a 91% probability of a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting, per CME’s FedWatch. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has gone so far as to call for a 50 basis point increase, saying the central bank needs to “shock people.”

Higher borrowing rates and tighter financial conditions would put further pressure on consumers and the wider economy, a worry for Donovan. He noted that inflationary concerns “focus on oil prices (which the Fed cannot influence) and perhaps AI-related demand (largely beyond the Fed’s reach). The only way to offset those would be to create near-recessionary conditions in the parts of the economy that respond to Fed action.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5414. Study: 403 U.S. data centers rival Denmark’s carbon emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

#5413. Exclusive: AWS Marketplace head on letting AI agents shop for software: “People can’t wait three months to get access to the latest one”

Amazon is rolling out a suite of AI agents to help companies purchase software and procure services on its AWS Marketplace product, including the ability to pre-authorize agents to take certain actions without having to wait for human approval.

Its latest Marketplace update gives people and AI agents tools for each stage of procurement, from finding products and reviewing contract terms to checking vendor security, making purchases and setting up supported software. Companies can give agents a budget to buy certain products and set rules for which purchases go to a person for approval.Say you ask an AI agent to build a company website. For the login page, many companies choose to select an outside vendor, such as Okta, to set up a sign-in service. The agent can find one that fits, but previously it might have had to wait for someone to approve the purchase before it could deploy and test that vendor’s solution.

“You shouldn’t have to approve that,” Matt Yanchyshyn, vice president of AWS Marketplace and partner services, told Fortune. The product manager who asked for the website to be built may not know which sign-in service to choose. After picking one, the agent should be able to start a free trial and perhaps pay for a month to build a real working prototype on a pay-as-you-go basis, he said.The way companies shop is already changing. “People aren’t searching with keywords anymore,” Yanchyshyn said, adding that AWS sees the shift in its own metrics. Instead of typing “database,” buyers describe what they want to build and what the software needs to do. An AI agent would handle this, turning a short prompt into a long list of requirements.Marketplace can use that description to recommend a mix of software and services for the project. Once buyers have a product in mind, they can ask the new checkout assistant how it’s priced, what the license allows and whether they may need a purchase order. AWS is also adding a category for data on Marketplace, saying AI agents increasingly use it. An agent evaluating a potential startup investment, for example, could pull funding data from Crunchbase.

So can agents buy on their own? Yanchyshyn said it’s up to each company. “If they want a human handoff on everything, fine,” he said. “But if they’re comfortable with a certain category of products to allow agents to make a purchase 100% independently, let’s let them. Because the most important thing right now in this climate is speed.” The buyer, he said, is responsible for setting those guardrails.

A company can give an agent permission to buy a tool and still need its IT team to check how the vendor handles company data. In a June 2026 survey by software review platform G2, 39% of the B2B software buyers it surveyed named IT security reviews as the biggest source of delay after choosing a vendor. AWS is working with Drata and Vanta, two compliance automation providers that help companies collect and share security and compliance evidence, to help buyers review vendors’ security records directly in Marketplace.Yanchyshyn said AI is making the need to buy software faster more urgent. Companies can’t afford to wait months for purchase decisions to clear security reviews, legal checks and budget approvals, he said. AI tools can change from one week to the next. “People can’t wait three months to get access to the latest one,” he said.

Adam Markowitz, co-founder and CEO of compliance platform Drata, told Fortune that a single security review can mean checking a vendor against 50 to 60 requirements, which might be distilled from a 100-line questionnaire. AI is adding to the list. “Now, with every vendor being an AI vendor, there’s a whole new set of criteria that security teams are assessing their vendors against,” he said. Done by hand, the process has meant weeks of back-and-forth. “Emails, requests, spreadsheets, questionnaires — the agent takes that down to minutes.”

An AI agent can pull the documents a vendor shares, such as a SOC 2 report, in which an outside auditor assesses a company’s security controls, and check them requirement by requirement, Markowitz said. For each one, the agent quotes the exact passage from the vendor’s documents that supports its conclusion, so a reviewer can check its work.

Bill Fitzgerald, vice president of global channel and alliances at Vanta, told Fortune that executives are trying to expand their use of AI while governing the tools and agents already inside their businesses. They’re asking, he said: “Are we leaning in hard enough to leverage the productivity and the impact of AI to drive and scale our business?”

Fitzgerald expects agents to take on more small, high-volume purchases fully autonomously. For seven-, eight- and nine-figure deals, he said, “you’re always going to have a human in the loop.”

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5412. Former UW AI researchers Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin raise $110M for AI startup Noeri

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company said.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

#5410. ‘Strict cell phone bans seem to plug about half of that leak’: Harvard economist finds locking up students’ phones adds 1–2 weeks of learning a year

Making students lock their phones in pouches for the school day adds one to two weeks of learning a year, according to a national study released Tuesday.

The study, from Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, with researchers at Dartmouth and the testing nonprofit NWEA, found that schools that required students to store their phones in pouches experienced an annual boost in achievement growth of 0.01 standard deviations—equivalent to 1–2 weeks of additional learning per year (or restoring two minutes per hour of class time). The team followed 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools across 49 states and Washington, D.C., from the 2021–22 through 2025–26 school years.

The gains are small, but they last. Achievement gains begin in the first year of the ban and appear to continue three years later, and the effect held across elementary, middle and high schools, and across rich and poor ones.

The result breaks with the last big study of school phone bans, which found in May that they did close to nothing for test scores. The argument has money riding on it: New York and 16 other states put bell-to-bell bans in place last school year, and Kane puts the cost of a pouch at about $25 a student.

That matters because of how far students have fallen. Tom Kane, an economist and education professor who serves as the director of Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, released an Education Scorecard which traced a “learning recession” back to 2013, years before the pandemic. Between 2013 and 2024, eighth-grade math and reading achievement fell by roughly one grade equivalent. The slide lines up with the spread of smartphones: in 2011, fewer than a quarter of teen students had access to smartphones. By 2018, 95% did.

“Strict cell phone bans seem to plug about half of that leak,” said Kane in a statement.

As for the other half, Kane told Fortune “the two main suspects are declining test-based accountability following the replacement of the No Child Left Behind Act and out-of-school social media use.” He added: “One of the big mysteries our study did not explain is the precipitous drop for the lowest achieving students. The abandonment of test-based accountability and out-of-school social media use could be most costly for them.”

A National Bureau of Economic Research study found in May that strict bans had close to zero effect on test scores. That team did find statistically significant gains with Yondr pouches in high school math, but those gains were offset by ban-related learning losses in middle school.

Tom Dee, a Stanford professor and co-author of that study, told NPR he considers the early results on phone bans “largely disappointing.” Neither study has been published in a peer-reviewed journal. The two also measured different things: the NBER study pooled school-level mean test scores at several thousand Yondr-adopting schools, while the Harvard study used student-level scores at the 844 schools that use both Yondr pouches and tests administered by NWEA.

Kane said the Harvard study, which is not a randomized trial, compared achievement growth at “roughly 800 Yondr-adopting schools before and after adoption against the achievement growth of 3800 matched comparison schools over the same time period.” He added, “The fact that the two groups of schools seemed to [be] following similar trends in the years before adoption made us more confident.”

The Harvard team flags its own limits too. It found signs that state-mandated bans in 22 states raised reading and math scores last year, but researchers cautioned that these findings might be confounded by pre-existing trends in the states implementing bans.

“Given the difference in post-pandemic recovery in the states with and without bans, it will be hard for anyone—not just us—to discern the effect of the bans by comparing across states,” Kane said. A better test, he said, would compare schools that already had strict bans of their own with schools in the same state that adopted bans only after the state law passed.

Kane’s pitch to districts is about money. “$25 is a small price to pay for an additional 1-2 weeks of instruction per student,” he said.

Advocates say the study confirms what schools have already seen. “Anecdotal evidence has already demonstrated that schools making the transition have the ability to change their school culture and bring face-to-face interaction back to the classroom and common areas like the cafeteria,” Ashwin Verghese, communications director at the children’s advocacy nonprofit Fairplay, told Fortune. “Now, the Harvard study is backing that up with evidence of steady educational gains.”

Julie Scelfo, a mother and the founder and executive director of Mothers Against Media Addiction, said the gains matter more than they sound. “It’s easy to forget that education is sequential, meaning that basic building blocks must be established before a child can go on to higher orders of learning,” she told Fortune. “So a week or two may not sound like much, but it actually adds up to quite a lot across a child’s K-12 education.” The benefit isn’t only academic, she added, but “the ability to focus and develop other executive functioning skills that are critical to every area of a child’s life.”

Scelfo acknowledged the study “doesn’t say much about phone and social media use after school,” but said the rise of smartphones and social media among young people tracks with what pediatric groups have declared a national emergency in child and adolescent mental health. “Parents should do everything possible to delay access to these products until safeguards are in place,” she said. She pointed to state laws such as the Age-Appropriate Design Code and New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act as models for other states.

New York City has banned, unbanned and rebanned phones in schools. The city’s ban dated to the late 1980s, but Bloomberg started strongly enforcing it in 2006. A small industry grew up around it: storage trucks outside schools charged students about $1 a day to hold their phones. One van owner in Far Rockaway told DNAinfo he netted around $160 to $170 per day. ​

In 2015, Mayor Bill de Blasio scrapped the ban, calling it “simply out of touch with the realities of modern day parenting,” according to CBS New York. He also called it unfair, because the ban was enforced mostly at schools with metal detectors in low-income neighborhoods.

A decade later, the city reversed course again. When Gov. Kathy Hochul signed the 2026 state budget into law on May 9, 2025, she made New York the largest state in the nation to restrict smartphones and other internet-enabled personal devices throughout the entire school day. New York was one of 17 states that adopted bell-to-bell bans for last school year.

The pouches at the center of the study weren’t built for classrooms. Graham Dugoni, a former professional soccer player, founded Yondr in 2014. He found early success with live performers, including comedian Dave Chappelle, who used the pouches to keep audiences from filming performances starting in 2015. A California high school was using them as early as 2019. More than 3,300 schools nationwide began using the pouches between the ‘19-‘20 and ‘25-‘26 school years.

The researchers say the bigger unknown is what students do with their phones outside school. They point to Meta’s $17 billion settlement with state attorneys general, which requires a block on app access between midnight and 6 a.m. and muted notifications during school hours (8 a.m. to 3 p.m.), excepting direct messages. The Harvard team wants states to encourage other platforms used by youth—YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, etc.—to adopt similar restrictions so students don’t simply switch apps.

Verghese said other platforms “should absolutely adopt the same limits, but they can’t stop there.” Fairplay was disappointed that the settlement does not turn off by default “recommendation algorithms that connect kids to predators and send young people down dangerous rabbit holes,” he said, and he argued it was “too focused on offering parents tools rather than restricting harmful features.” He added: “Even if other companies adopted these restrictions, two hours per day on four or five different platforms adds up to far too much time.”

“What families really need is for Congress to pass comprehensive legislation that will force companies like Meta to stop designing for addiction and make their products safer by default,” Verghese said, calling on lawmakers to pass the Kids Online Safety Act in the coming weeks.

Teodora Pavkovic, director of wellbeing and parent advocacy at Qustodio and Aura Parents, which make parental-control apps, told Fortune that a school-day ban “only addresses a fraction of students’ digital lives, leaving the hours outside school largely untouched.” Aura Parents’ 2026 State of the Youth Report found that sleep is the single strongest predictor of a teen’s digital wellbeing. “Teens with low wellbeing spend three times more time on their devices overnight, pick up their phones seven times more often, and take twice as long to disengage after bedtime,” Pavkovic said.

Kids don’t fully make up for lost screen time after school, Pavkovic said, “but they do pack their social lives into those hours.” Among nearly 30,000 children ages 7 to 17 in Aura’s data, about a third use their devices during school hours. By 3 p.m., more than 60% do. “School phone bans are a helpful starting point, but they need to be paired with healthy boundaries at home, like keeping phones out of bedrooms at night,” she said.

Kane says he now wants to study students’ smartphone and social media use outside of school.

Binance said on Monday, November 16, that it will pass the next Microsoft and Applied Materials cash dividends to holders of its tokenized stocks, MSFTB and AMATB. It will snapshot balances on Thursday, November 19, the same day both stocks go ex-dividend.

Tokenized stocks are crypto tokens that track a real share, held by a custodian, and trade around the clock. Binance’s versions, called bStocks, do not pay the dividend in cash. Instead, the net amount is reinvested, and each holder’s token balance grows slightly.

We compared both tokens with the real shares since late August. During market hours, they tracked closely. Over weekends, their price called Monday’s opening move only half the time.

Here is what holders get, and what the token prices tell traders this week.

Both companies declared their payouts in September. Microsoft will pay $0.98 a share, up from $0.91. Applied Materials, a maker of chipmaking equipment, will pay $0.53 a share. Both go to shareholders of record on November 19 and are paid on December 10.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

Binance does not state the tax rate. The standard U.S. rate on dividends paid to foreign holders without a tax treaty is 30%. At that rate, we worked out what holders get:

A dividend only matters if the token tracks the stock. So we compared both tokens with the real shares, using Binance hourly candles and Nasdaq prices since late August.

During market hours, the match is close. At the Nasdaq close, the tokens sat at a median 0.06% from the official closing price across 58 sessions. The widest gap was 0.28%.

Weekends are different. The tokens keep trading while Wall Street is shut, so we checked whether their weekend price predicted Monday’s opening move.

Thin trading in tokenized stocks explains part of it. MSFTB traded about $183,000 in the past 24 hours on Binance, and AMATB about $114,000. This weekend, AMATB stood 1.8% below Friday’s $370.50 close on Sunday night, while MSFTB was down 0.2%. On our numbers, those weekend quotes said little about where the stocks would open.

On the 4-hour chart, where each candle covers four hours, MSFTB trades at $527.61 on Binance. It sits just above its 50-period exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $526.02, and its 200-period EMA at $526.95. With both averages flat and close together, the trend is neutral.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

For holders of tokenized stocks, the dividend adds about a tenth of a percent to their balance this quarter. The bigger lesson is in timing: on weekdays, the tokens follow the stock, but weekend prices are a weak guide to Monday.

#5408. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5407. Portland startup Fairly raises $22M to pair local caretakers with AI for vacation rentals

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon said in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”

Breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.
