#5406. Radian Aerospace plans to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey said he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”

Greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small company.

Humphrey said the company currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

So, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey said. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”

He acknowledged that following through on the plan for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace company? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”

#5405. Booking Holdings’ travel startup Vayo starts booking trips with AI agents, even on rival Expedia

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup launched by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel plans — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of users in its invite-only beta.

That includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The company says Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

Vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, said last month that it plans to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

Companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

When Vayo launched last month, Fridgen said it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo says no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s new booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister company Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

For flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the company says.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

Vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the company says. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever company they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

The service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

His co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the company says it plans to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

#5404. Seattle fleet tracking company Zonar names Atlanta-based CEO, who says HQ is staying put

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking company, has a new CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no plans to change that.” He said he visits the company’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

Consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based company acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software company Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and says it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli said Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

Zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but said Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by new pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Zonar has added 1,000 new customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 plan, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli said.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli said. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”

Founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

#5403. The Pizza Hut Founder Who Turned a $600 Loan From Mom Into an 18,000-Location Empire Dies at 95

Before the famous red roofs, Dan Carney and his brother started selling franchises just one year after opening in Wichita.

Franchise legend Dan Carney died on November 13 at age 95. Carney co-founded the original Pizza Hut, which grew into one of the world’s largest franchise systems, with 18,642 locations today.

It all started with a magazine article and a $600 loan from his mother. After reading about the growing popularity of a new food sensation called “pizza,” Carney, then 26, and his younger brother, Frank, opened a small pizza joint in Wichita, Kansas, in 1958, CNN reports. It sat on the same corner where their father once ran a grocery store. A year later, the brothers opened their first franchise in Topeka. They expanded overseas in 1970, and in 1977 they sold the chain to PepsiCo for $300 million.

Carney gave franchisees much of the credit. When the original building reopened in 2018 as the Pizza Hut Museum on the Wichita State University campus, he said it honored those who “shared risks and ambition in building a global organization.”

Carney also chaired the Cerebral Palsy Research Foundation of Kansas for more than 50 years. “When you win at something, you owe something back to the community,” he once said.

#5402. Strategy Slows Its Bitcoin Buying as MSTR Stock Slides: Why Has Saylor Eased Off?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Strategy said on Monday, November 16, that it bought 485 Bitcoin last week for $33.4 million, less than half of the 1,036 BTC it bought the week before. MSTR stock fell 6% at Monday’s open to about $105 as Michael Saylor’s company, which now holds 850,849 BTC, slowed its buying.

The same filing shows where most of the money went. Strategy spent $228.1 million buying back its own preferred stock, STRC, nearly seven times what it spent on Bitcoin.

Strategy has acquired 485 $BTC and repurchased $228M of $STRC. As of 11/15/26, we hold 850,849 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets. $MSTR https://t.co/9dZBx810Wi

We added up Strategy’s weekly filings since mid-October. Over five weeks, it spent about $1 billion on preferred buybacks and about $200 million on Bitcoin. MSTR stock, Strategy’s common shares, fell 6% at Monday’s open to about $105. Bitcoin itself trades near $65,000, down 21% since early October.

So why are Strategy’s Bitcoin buys slowing, and what is MSTR stock doing?

Explore: Binance Pays Microsoft and Applied Materials Dividends on Tokenized Stocks: How Much Holders Get

Strategy reports its purchases every Monday in a filing with the SEC called an 8-K. Its latest filing covers November 9 to 15. We lined it up with the four before it.

STRC, nicknamed “Stretch,” is a preferred share that pays a monthly dividend and is meant to trade near $100. It fell to about $85 in July and is back at $99.60, close to that target. Buying it back cuts Strategy’s dividend bill, which runs at about $1.43 billion a year across all its preferred shares.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

The second reason is the price of MSTR stock itself. Strategy pays for most purchases by selling new MSTR shares. That works best when the stock trades well above the value of the Bitcoin behind each share.

Strategy’s own dashboard puts that ratio, called mNAV, at 1.11. At that level, selling shares adds little Bitcoin per share, so each new share does less for existing holders. Last week, Strategy sold $244.7 million of MSTR, but only $33.4 million of it went into Bitcoin.

MSTR stock has fallen faster than Bitcoin:

There is also a limit on the buybacks. Strategy has $332.2 million left under its preferred repurchase program, less than two weeks at the current pace. Once it runs out, Strategy has to choose between raising the limit and moving that money back to Bitcoin.

On the daily chart of Hyperliquid’s 24/7 MSTR contract, the stock trades at $104.75. It sits below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $131.98, and its 200-day EMA at $133.37.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

Strategy has not stopped buying Bitcoin, but it has changed its priorities. For MSTR stock, next Monday’s filing is the one to watch. A bigger Bitcoin buy would show the cash is moving back to Bitcoin. Another week dominated by STRC would point the other way.

#5401. Glenn Kelman’s next act: Former Redfin CEO takes on health care with stealthy startup Sojourn

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software company, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

His co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health plans that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

Kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their plans “after we’ve built our product.”

But after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the plan.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

“Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it says.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site says, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”

Kelman, by his own account, is new to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman said the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software company he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in new blood.”

The Sojourn site says the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”

That fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn plans to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”

A new health plan typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the company hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a new mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He said at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

#5400. I Grew My LinkedIn Following From 6,000 to More Than 520,000 in 3 Years. Here’s the Simple System Any Founder Can Use.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

My LinkedIn growth didn’t come from luck, but from a simple loop any founder can repeat.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Ask a room of founders whether LinkedIn matters for their business, and most hands go up. Ask how many of them posted last week, and the room gets quiet.

The reasons are familiar: no time, nothing worth saying, fear of sounding self-promotional. So the profile stays silent until there’s a launch to announce. By then, nobody is listening.

That silence has a cost. Edelman and LinkedIn research found that 95% of potential business clients aren’t looking to buy at any given moment. When a need comes up, they turn to names they already know.

I learned this the slow way. Three years ago, my LinkedIn account had about 6,000 followers. Today it has more than 520,000 followers and connections. That growth came from the same loop we use at BetterMe: test, learn, improve, scale.

List the areas where you have firsthand experience, and keep the two or three you’ll never get tired of learning about. Before you publish, ask whether the post helps readers understand one of them through your experience. Over time, readers connect those subjects with your name. That’s what turns a passing visitor into a follower.

Mine are entrepreneurship, leadership and personal wellness. I rarely have to hunt for material. A product decision, a mistake, a comment on a previous post or a customer question usually becomes my next post.

Change one element per post, whether that’s the hook, the length, the format or the time of day, and compare the response. This takes the guesswork and ego out of publishing.

At BetterMe, we treat testing as the fastest way to learn what people actually want. I brought that same mindset to content. Some of my early posts were far from perfect, but every quiet post became a data point, and every harsh comment became free feedback. I’m a proud member of my own haters’ fan club.

Pick a rhythm you can maintain for months. If daily feels like too much, start with three posts a week for a month.

Consistency gives readers a reason to come back, and the platform rewards it. Buffer analyzed more than 2 million LinkedIn posts and found that going from one post a week to two to five can mean about 1,182 more impressions per post.

My early mistake was posting only about big wins, then disappearing for months. Every comeback started from zero. The turning point came when I committed to posting every day, weekends included.

People decide in seconds whether to keep reading. When I edit, I cut anything a tired reader would skip. One of my recent LinkedIn posts is a typical example of how I structure mine.

Adapt popular trends to your expertise and the subjects you write about. New readers find you through the format, and your perspective brings them back.

Before adopting a trend, I ask what it can help me explain: a leadership lesson, a habit I’ve built, a hard decision or a mistake I’ve made. If the format makes that lesson easier to follow, I use it.

LinkedIn isn’t only a place to publish. It’s a network, and your future clients, investors and partners are probably already on it. You just haven’t met them yet.

So build your network proactively. Publish first, then reach out with a short message: why you chose this person, a post of theirs that caught your attention and one specific question. For people outside your network, LinkedIn Premium Business includes 15 InMail credits a month, so you can start that conversation directly.

Your content makes those messages easier to answer. An Edelman-LinkedIn report found that nine in 10 decision-makers are more receptive to outreach from companies that consistently publish thought leadership. This approach helped me connect with journalists, and some of them later came back to me with interview and comment requests.

Follower count is the easiest number to track and the least useful one. Instead, watch who joins the discussion, which contacts come back and whether a conversation leads to a meaningful next step. Those signals show whether you’re reaching the people you hope to work with.

In my experience, a few readers who comment thoughtfully and keep coming back say more about my reach than thousands of silent new followers.

Visibility on LinkedIn isn’t a talent or a lucky break. It’s a system you can build.

You’ll never feel ready, so don’t wait for it. Pick one subject, write one useful post and have one real conversation with someone who responds. Then note who replied and what you’d change, and let that note shape your next post.

Before you write that post, take a look at LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook for practical ways to build your brand and grow your network. Then explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to help your content and outreach go further.

Three years ago, I was posting into silence. The only thing that changed was that I kept running the loop. Somewhere in your network, a future client, partner or hire isn’t looking for you yet. When they are, make sure yours is the name they already know.

Ask a room of founders whether LinkedIn matters for their business, and most hands go up. Ask how many of them posted last week, and the room gets quiet.

The reasons are familiar: no time, nothing worth saying, fear of sounding self-promotional. So the profile stays silent until there’s a launch to announce. By then, nobody is listening.

That silence has a cost. Edelman and LinkedIn research found that 95% of potential business clients aren’t looking to buy at any given moment. When a need comes up, they turn to names they already know.

#5399. Stop Memorizing Metrics. This One Ratio Is All That Matters For Your Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Learn how the relationship between customer lifetime value and acquisition cost can guide smarter decisions about growth.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

There is one ratio that determines whether your business will thrive or starve. The whole health and success of your business can be reduced to two numbers on either side of a colon.

What is this all-encompassing equation? Well, it’s simply the ratio of lifetime value (LTV) of your average customer compared to your average customer acquisition cost (CAC).

Entrepreneurs are constantly urged to “know their numbers.” Ultimately, it all rests on the relationship between lifetime value and customer acquisition cost.

Lifetime value is the actual profit you make per customer, and as long as the lifetime value per customer exceeds the cost to acquire that customer, your business has a future. If the lifetime value of your average customer is not larger than the average customer acquisition cost, then that business is doomed.

I was once on an innovation council for Lower Mississippi, and we did a Shark Tank-like competition where business owners pitched their business ideas. One of the ideas that everyone seemed enamored with was a sticker for the back of phones that could be rubbed to calm a person down in a highly tense setting. It was clinically proven, they said, to reduce anxiety in the moment. However, the reality is that no one is going to pay more than $5 for what is basically a piece of sticky sandpaper for the back of the phone.

When I raised that objection, it was pointed out to me that the cost of making that sticker was only $2, which gave this product seemingly healthy margins.

However, the reason I could see instantly that this idea had no future is because there is no environment where you can tell a story, like this product required, and achieve less than a $5 customer acquisition cost. In fact, what they needed was, at minimum, a large retail endcap or countertop display that had visuals and testimonials telling the story of what this thing does, or a paid social media campaign to tell the story of what the product is, how it works and the benefits of using it.

The problem is that both avenues are more likely to result in a customer acquisition cost exceeding $20. This means that rather than the product selling for $5, it needs to be priced in the $30 to $40 range to yield a profit, which for a scratchy sticker just doesn’t seem reasonable.

On average, you typically want at least a 3:1 ratio of lifetime value to customer acquisition cost. This would effectively mean that for every dollar you put into growing the business, you are getting three dollars in return. That’s a comfortable enough ratio to make almost any business sustainable for the long run.

The reason this ratio is so important to know is that it gives you a very real understanding of your business’s true scalability. If you’re debating taking on debt for your business, the only way to know whether or not that debt is a good decision is knowing if that debt is going towards something that has a long-term chance of success.

As long as you can acquire customers at a lower cost than what you make from those customers, then you have a business that can be taken as far as the natural limits of your industry allow.

Lifetime value is the average profit per order multiplied by the average purchase frequency over time. Even though technically “lifetime” means exactly that, for practical reasons I never calculate it longer than three years.  That may seem arbitrary, and it is, but no one is a customer forever, so three years seems like the best timeframe to cap “lifetime,” in my opinion.

So, if your average order is $5,000 and your average profit margin is 20%, your average profit per order is $1,000. Let’s say that typically someone only buys from you once every 10 years or so; then, effectively, your lifetime value is $1,000 ($1,000 profit × 1 frequency = $1,000).

Conversely, let’s say that you were selling a monthly subscription at $20 per month with a 50% profit margin, and you know that your average customer lifecycle is two years, then your lifetime value is $240 ($10 profit × 24 months = $240).

Customer acquisition cost can be a little trickier to calculate for most businesses. You may have an ice cream stand set up on the beach with a handwritten sign and you effectively have a customer acquisition cost of almost zero. On the other hand, you may have a large sales team that travels around the world going to conferences and working trade shows, combined with massive advertising campaigns.

However, the reality is that the actual math behind this number is relatively simple. Add up your marketing and sales costs, and divide that number by the number of new customers you have.

If you spent $2 million in sales and marketing expenses over the past year, and you gained 2,000 new customers, then your average customer acquisition cost is $1,000 ($2,000,000 ÷ 2,000 = $1,000).

Should you lower your operational costs? To a point, yes, but eventually lowering cost hurts the customer experience which can increase customer acquisition cost and/or lower the lifetime gross profit of each customer by increasing churn. Should you invest more in your advertising efforts? It depends on what your customer acquisition cost is from those campaigns and whether it is less than your lifetime value.

Know your LTV and your CAC by heart. These two numbers are either the linchpin upon which your entire business is built, or the nail in the coffin of why your business fails.

There is one ratio that determines whether your business will thrive or starve. The whole health and success of your business can be reduced to two numbers on either side of a colon.

What is this all-encompassing equation? Well, it’s simply the ratio of lifetime value (LTV) of your average customer compared to your average customer acquisition cost (CAC).

Entrepreneurs are constantly urged to “know their numbers.” Ultimately, it all rests on the relationship between lifetime value and customer acquisition cost.

#5398. Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am

Update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA said Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

That stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA said. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based company hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and New Glenn for our return to flight.”

Impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has said it plans to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

#5397. Microsoft’s CEO Says Employees Shoud Follow This Transformative Career Advice

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s what the tech leader wants engineers to keep in mind as they plan their next move.

Microsoft’s chief executive has advice for navigating a software engineering career in the age of AI.

On an episode of The Pragmatic Engineer podcast this week, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella had a suggestion for software engineers worried about AI: He advised them to gain experience with the work done with it.

For engineers just starting their careers, that means joining a team that is building with the technology, he said. He encouraged people to spend more time gaining practical experience and less time following the conversation around AI.

“It’s just not about the hype cycle and that constant need to talk,” Nadella said in an interview with podcast host Gergely Orosz, who is a software engineer and author. “But it’s do more, learn more and hands-on experience — experience it firsthand.”

Nadella added that nothing could beat hands-on learning and working alongside people putting AI to use. He said those tactics were more valuable than any other approach, whether someone was a recent graduate, a mid-career professional or a CEO like him.

“The more you can take the time to sort of learn to do, be in teams that are doing, the better it is versus, I think, anything else,” Nadella said.

The job market offers a mixed picture compared to Nadella’s advice. Software engineering hiring is picking up, but the recovery favors experienced workers.

Senior-level roles accounted for 69.3% of U.S. software development postings in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 54.5% in early 2019, according to Indeed data.

Nadella also put the focus on employers, saying companies should give junior engineers more chances to develop their skills as AI reshapes software engineering.

“I care a lot about, hey, can you have an early-career person come in, join one of these teams, go up the learning curve,” Nadella said. “So what’s the new form of that is what I think we have to really discover.”

Other tech leaders have argued that businesses still need to invest in people at the start of their careers. Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said on The Big Interview podcast last year that cutting off entry-level hiring would undermine the talent pipeline companies need to survive.

“If you have no talent pipeline that you’re building and no junior people that you’re mentoring and bringing up through the company, we often find that that’s where we get some of the best ideas,” he said.

Garman also challenged the assumption that experienced workers necessarily use the technology more effectively.

“Many of the most junior folks are actually the most experienced with the AI tools,” he said. “So they’re actually most able to get the most out of them.”

IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has also pushed back on the idea that AI means fewer opportunities for graduates. “I expect we are probably going to hire more people out of college over the next 12 months than we have in the past few years,” he told CNN in October 2025.

#5396. I Built More Trust in 10 Minutes in a Sauna Than in Months of Coffee Meetings

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Ten minutes in a sauna can do the work of months of coffee meetings. Here’s what the research says about why, plus tips for getting started.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I recently met a venture fund founder in the sauna at the Ritz-Carlton in Dallas. We spent about 10 minutes together and got deep into science and tech in the wellness world. We also spoke about taking care of our aging parents. We got further in those 10 minutes than most people do in months of coffee meetings, and we’ve stayed in touch ever since.

I don’t play golf, but I know plenty of business still gets done on the course. For me, the most honest business and personal conversations happen half-naked, sweating and uncomfortable. It’s the truth, literally.

In 2023, I wrote here that a sauna session could leave you primed to negotiate or close a deal. I’ve since changed my mind about the order of operations. The sauna doesn’t help you close. It helps you trust, and the deals follow.

CNN recently named a sauna as Barcelona’s hottest new nightlife spot, with a spa turning into a rave for 100 people built around wellness and sobriety. London’s ARC opened with a 65-person sauna and DJ sets. In New York, The Altar planned a 50-person sauna on Fifth Avenue.

Clubs aren’t disappearing, but the job they did for us, getting adults to drop their guard together, now has a new home. Only 54% of U.S. adults say they drink, matching the lowest level Gallup has recorded since 1939. I’ve written about what that means for beverage founders and why recovery has become a KPI. What interests me now is what happens inside the room.

There’s a reason for what Gabby Reece called “the truth barrel,” the name of an older podcast she recorded in a sauna. It’s hard to perform when you’re half-dressed and dripping. There are no phones and nothing to hide behind. Everyone in the room is equally uncomfortable, and nobody’s title matters much after five minutes.

When I sat in the most spacious sauna I’ve ever seen, at Love.Life in Los Angeles, the benches were full of pro athletes, coaches, trainers and founders comparing notes on our days and how we try to balance it all. More recently, I spent time in a 175-degree sauna at The Assembly Retreat, getting to know familiar faces and new connections alike. I’m a member of The Assembly, a network of investors, founders and operators in health and wellness, and those were some of the most intimate business and personal conversations I’ve had. No selling, no suits — except bathing suits. People help each other and tell the truth, and deal flow follows because you want to work with people you trust.

The research points the same way. A 2026 paper covering 1,907 sauna users in the U.K. tied weekly sauna use to better self-reported physical and mental health, and belonging explained part of that link. The authors also linked ritual and shared emotion to stronger bonds. It’s self-reported data from people already into sauna culture, but it matches what I’ve experienced.

I’ve learned that trust rarely gets built across a table. Sit somewhere hot with someone, or sweat with them, and don’t sell them anything.

The science is part of why I love the sauna and make it part of my routine three to four times a week. In a Finnish study of 2,315 men followed for about 20 years, those using a sauna four to seven times a week had a 50% lower risk of fatal cardiovascular disease than once-a-week users. A later study of 1,688 adults, about half of them women, found that the most frequent users had roughly a quarter of the rate of fatal cardiovascular events seen in once-weekly users. It’s not proof, but it’s enough to keep me on the bench.

It can also help you get more out of your workout. In an eight-week randomized trial of 47 inactive adults, adding a 15-minute sauna after exercise improved fitness, systolic blood pressure and total cholesterol more than exercise alone. Blood pressure fell an additional 8 mmHg. Exercise physiologist Dr. Stacy Sims writes about why heat training matters for women in particular.

For mental health, the evidence is still early but promising. A small sham-controlled trial found that whole-body heat held promise for depression, though it used a medical heating setup, not a sauna. I don’t treat it as a cure. As I’ve written before, wellness shouldn’t feel like a second job. I keep the sauna because it’s one of the few health habits that also gives me time with people.

I prefer a traditional barrel sauna over infrared. Infrared warms up faster, but sessions run longer, and the long-term mortality research centers on traditional saunas. Saunas have been around for thousands of years, and I like that this one still works much the way it always has.

I keep mine at about 175°F and stay for 20 minutes. The workout trial above used about 175 to 179°F, and the Finnish data favored sessions longer than 19 minutes. If you’re new, start shorter and build up. Most important, listen to your body.

Wear a hat to keep your head cooler so you can stay longer, and stick with natural fibers. The truest way to sauna is “no textiles,” but that’s tough to pull off with other people. Drink water, skip alcohol and cool down at your own pace. Check with your doctor first if you have a heart condition or any other health concern.

The conversation that matters most to me happens in my own backyard. My husband and I have about two sauna dates a week. Along with our non-negotiable long walk on Sundays, it’s where we connect and catch up.

The nightclub gave us a place to lose ourselves. The sauna gives us a place to be found out, and that turns out to be the better deal.

I recently met a venture fund founder in the sauna at the Ritz-Carlton in Dallas. We spent about 10 minutes together and got deep into science and tech in the wellness world. We also spoke about taking care of our aging parents. We got further in those 10 minutes than most people do in months of coffee meetings, and we’ve stayed in touch ever since.

I don’t play golf, but I know plenty of business still gets done on the course. For me, the most honest business and personal conversations happen half-naked, sweating and uncomfortable. It’s the truth, literally.

In 2023, I wrote here that a sauna session could leave you primed to negotiate or close a deal. I’ve since changed my mind about the order of operations. The sauna doesn’t help you close. It helps you trust, and the deals follow.

#5394. Struggling to Get Business Referrals? Here’s the Hurdle You May Not Realize You’re Creating.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Your network may be full of people who trust you. But trust alone doesn’t generate referrals. Here’s what most entrepreneurs overlook.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I attend my share of networking events, and there’s one question I hear almost every time: “Who would be a good referral for you?”

It’s a fair question. But the answers usually sound something like this: business owners, CEOs, companies looking to grow or anyone who needs marketing.

I understand the instinct. Nobody wants to limit their opportunities. But think about the person listening. They might know hundreds of business owners. How are they supposed to recognize which one actually needs your help?

I’ve learned that people don’t necessarily need more reminders to refer you. They need a clearer reason to think of you in the first place.

And there’s something else entrepreneurs often overlook. When someone makes an introduction, they’re not just sharing a contact. They’re putting their own reputation behind that recommendation.

Let’s say you’ve known someone professionally for several years. You enjoy their company, respect their work and would happily meet them for coffee. Does that automatically mean you’d recommend them to an important client? Probably not.

You would want to know whether they could deliver, how they treated customers and whether making the introduction might put an existing relationship at risk. Your professional network makes those same judgments about you.

This is why I don’t believe referrals should be treated as a numbers game. Having 500 contacts doesn’t mean you have 500 people willing to recommend your business. A smaller network of people who understand your expertise and trust how you operate may be far more valuable.

The real question isn’t how many people know you. It’s how many would feel comfortable putting their credibility behind you.

One mistake I see entrepreneurs make is describing their businesses too broadly.

“We offer comprehensive consulting services.”

These statements might be accurate, but they’re difficult for someone else to use. A better approach is to explain the situation that typically brings a customer to you.

For example, a business owner might say, “We work with companies that are generating plenty of leads but struggling to turn those inquiries into customers.”

Now the person listening has something specific to recognize. They may remember a conversation with a founder complaining about poor conversion or a colleague frustrated with marketing spending that isn’t producing results.

You haven’t asked them to memorize your service offerings. You’ve helped them identify a problem.

I made a related argument in my Entrepreneur article about businesses spending more on marketing while attracting fewer customers. Businesses can create plenty of activity without attracting the right opportunities.

The same is true of networking. More introductions aren’t necessarily better if the people being introduced don’t need what you provide.

I’ve come to think of referrals as an extension of relationship marketing, where familiarity, credibility and genuine understanding matter more than the number of people reached. That distinction is explored in this discussion of relationship marketing for service-based businesses.

The underlying idea is straightforward: Someone needs a reason to trust your judgment before they’re comfortable sharing that trust with another person.

For entrepreneurs, that confidence is built through ordinary professional behavior. Do you follow through when you promise something? Are you transparent about what you can and cannot deliver? Do you treat smaller opportunities with the same care as larger ones?

And when someone introduces a potential customer, do you take the time to understand their needs, or do you immediately launch into a sales pitch?

People remember those experiences. They also remember when an introduction leaves them embarrassed.

If you want more referrals, protecting the confidence of the person making the introduction should be as important as winning the potential customer.

Here’s another question worth asking: Have you made it easy for someone to explain why your business is different?

Too often, entrepreneurs hand people a website or a long presentation and expect them to figure it out. I would rather give someone one useful observation they can remember and repeat.

Suppose you’re an accountant who helps growing businesses understand why profitability is declining despite increasing sales. You might explain that many companies focus on revenue without examining what each additional sale actually contributes to profit. That’s a conversation starter.

Someone who hears a business owner discussing shrinking margins can recognize the connection without having to understand every service you offer.

Being visible and being selected are different challenges. Referrals bring that distinction into focus. Someone can know your business exists without understanding why they should recommend it. Your responsibility is to close that gap.

There is something uncomfortable about networking relationships that feel entirely transactional.

You introduce someone to a prospective customer and immediately wonder when they’ll return the favor. You send a helpful article and expect a sales opportunity. You attend an event and measure success by the number of business cards collected.

I’ve never believed strong professional relationships work particularly well that way. Some connections lead to business quickly. Others develop over years. Many never result in a transaction, and that’s perfectly fine.

I prefer to focus on whether I can make a useful connection, share something relevant or help someone think differently about a challenge.

That doesn’t mean abandoning commercial discipline. Keep track of conversations. Follow up when you’ve promised to. Understand which relationships are relevant to your business.

But don’t confuse relationship management with treating every interaction as a potential invoice. People can tell the difference.

Instead of introducing yourself by listing your services, describe one situation in which your business genuinely makes a difference. Keep it specific enough that someone could recognize it in a conversation with a friend or colleague.

Then ask three people you trust to explain what they think your business does. Don’t help them answer. Listen to the language they use and the problems they associate with you. If their answers are vague or completely different, that’s useful information. Your positioning may be less clear than you think.

Next, consider what happens after someone makes an introduction. Do you respond promptly? Do you acknowledge the person who connected you? Do you handle the conversation in a way that reinforces their confidence?

These small details determine whether someone will feel comfortable recommending you again.

Entrepreneurs spend considerable time trying to become more visible. We invest in marketing, attend events, publish content and build professional networks. Those efforts matter. But there’s a difference between being known and being recommended.

You can’t demand someone’s trust, and you can’t manufacture a meaningful referral through repeated requests. You can, however, make your expertise easier to understand, consistently deliver on your commitments and treat every introduction with care.

Before your next networking event, I’d encourage you to stop asking how many people you can meet. Ask yourself something more useful: If someone recommended me to a person they deeply respect, would I make them glad they did?

That’s the standard worth building a business around.

I attend my share of networking events, and there’s one question I hear almost every time: “Who would be a good referral for you?”

It’s a fair question. But the answers usually sound something like this: business owners, CEOs, companies looking to grow or anyone who needs marketing.

I understand the instinct. Nobody wants to limit their opportunities. But think about the person listening. They might know hundreds of business owners. How are they supposed to recognize which one actually needs your help?

#5393. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5391. Seattle tech vet and Sounders FC minority owner Chee Chew joins front office to lead AI push

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club announced Tuesday.

“His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer said in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

“In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”

Chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years. It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

Chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew said, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew said he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he said.

#5389. I Built an AI Chatbot for $0. Here’s the Exact Stack.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

You don’t need money to ship a real, production-grade AI chatbot. You need to know which free tiers to stack. Here’s the exact toolchain.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I also built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot, and it cost me $0.

From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. Here’s the stack I actually used to build it layer by layer, what I did with each tool and what’s free about it.

Before writing a line of code, a chatbot needs a face. I used Figma to generate the chatbot’s logo straight from a text prompt describing the style and mood I wanted, then iterated on it a few times inside Figma itself rather than handing it to a designer. Figma’s own free plan covers individual use with unlimited file storage.

The whole project lives in a GitHub repository, private while the chatbot was still rough, and it’s the same repo both Claude and Codex connect to. GitHub’s free plan gives unlimited private repositories with a limited feature set and 2,000 minutes a month of Actions included on GitHub Free for standard runners on private repos, enough to run tests and basic automation without hitting a wall. Standard runners on public repositories stay free no matter how much you use them.

Claude Code did the actual building, the chatbot’s backend and the AI agents running inside it. I kept it connected directly to the GitHub repository and never let it touch the main branch directly: every task ran on its own branch, and nothing merged until I’d reviewed the diff myself and approved the pull request. The genuine free route in is a Guest Pass: if someone you know already pays for Claude Max, they can send you one, and it unlocks a full week of free Pro-level access.

I gave Codex a different job, connected to the same repository but never writing production code itself. It reviewed what Claude had actually shipped, acting as an independent judge on pull requests, and I also used it to draft the next development prompt I’d hand back to Claude, effectively having one model plan the work and another execute it. Codex has a genuine free plan at $0 a month. Free accounts run on GPT-5.6 Terra, OpenAI’s cost-efficient model for that tier. The free plan is capped at a usage limit rather than a time limit, which is exactly the size of job a reviewer role needs.

I bought the chatbot’s domain name through Cloudflare, where registration is usually cheap since Cloudflare sells at cost with no markup, and kept the DNS in the same place rather than splitting it across providers. From there I used Cloudflare’s free security layer to protect the domain, including rate limiting rules to stop any single source from hammering the chatbot’s endpoints. Cloudflare’s WAF documentation covers exactly this kind of rule, and the core protections, DNS, DDoS protection, and basic security features, are included on the free plan.

I used Railway for both the backend and the frontend, with a separate test environment so I could ship changes quickly without risking the live version. New accounts get a one-time free credit grant before any card is required, and unlike some free hosts, Railway doesn’t put your service to sleep by default the way its own documentation describes for its optional Serverless feature, so there’s no cold start tax on the free tier unless you turn that behavior on yourself.

Users sign up and log in through Clerk, and I built the whole flow using Clerk’s own test environment first, so I could try edge cases without creating real accounts or sending real emails. The free plan covers up to 50,000 monthly active users at no cost, which is more than enough room to move from testing into a real launch on the same setup.

Conversations, users and application data all sit in Neon, a serverless Postgres database that scales down to zero and stops costing anything the moment nobody’s using it. The free tier includes enough storage and monthly compute hours for a real early product, with no credit card required to start.

Once the chatbot’s AI agents were actually running, I needed to see what they were doing under the hood: which prompts fired, where they failed, and what they cost. Langfuse traces all of that, and its free Hobby plan includes a healthy monthly allowance of tracing events, enough to debug and monitor a real chatbot without paying anything.

I wired Exa and Firecrawl directly into the AI agents responsible for research inside the chatbot’s runtime, so the chatbot itself can decide when it needs to look something up. Exa handles the search, finding relevant pages for a given question, and its free tier hands new accounts starting credit plus a recurring monthly allowance with no payment method required. It also ships a playground where you can test a search query directly in the browser before wiring it into your agent. Firecrawl handles what comes next, turning a page Exa found into clean text the agent can actually read, and its own free plan includes a monthly credit allowance with no card needed either.

Before committing to a specific model for the chatbot’s agents, I used NVIDIA’s API Catalog to try several without paying per token. NVIDIA gives any developer free credits to test a wide range of hosted models through its own endpoints, which made it easy to compare options before locking in whichever one actually powers the chatbot in production.

The chatbot talks back, not just types, so I used Azure AI Speech for text to speech, letting the chatbot switch between a female or male neural voice depending on the setup. The free tier includes a real monthly allowance of neural voice characters at no cost, enough for genuine daily conversations before you’d ever see a bill.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m currently building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds. I also built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot, and it cost me $0.

From the outside, it looks like a simple chatbot. Under the hood, it’s a distributed system that has to handle the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. #5388. Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am

Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

It’s a big upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD said a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

The machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the company’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. New York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a new name, SPD said, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”

#5387. Anthropic’s $81 Billion IPO Is the Biggest Ever — Here’s Who’s Getting Rich and Who Missed Out

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude is now a $2 trillion public company. Not everyone is happy.

Anthropic, the company behind the popular AI chatbot, surged more than 30% in its Nasdaq debut today after the largest IPO in history. It sold more than 980 million shares at $83 apiece for $81.3 billion, topping the then-record $75 billion SpaceX raised in June, according to The New York Times. Shares opened at $111.50 under the ticker “ANT,” valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion.

The biggest winners of the Anthropic IPO are the company’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, president Daniela Amodei. Each holds a stake that could be worth $20 billion or more, according to the Times. On the VC side, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Iconiq hold stakes worth more than $25 billion at the IPO price, The Wall Street Journal reports. Menlo Ventures’ stake is worth roughly $22.5 billion. Amazon, Google and Gulf sovereign wealth funds are also in line for huge paydays.

Then there’s Sam Bankman-Fried. The FTX founder led Anthropic’s $580 million Series B in 2022. After FTX collapsed, its bankruptcy estate sold the $500 million stake in 2024 for about $1.3 billion. At the IPO price, those shares would be worth roughly $37 billion today. China was also locked out of the offering.
